strategicHypothesis.aiDraft:
test-1 stands at a critical strategic inflection point. As a government organization with a strong foundational base — including clear governance structures, committed leadership, and an established market presence — test-1 is well-positioned to transition from a reactive, compliance-driven model to a proactive, value-creating institution.

The diagnostic reveals a consistent pattern: test-1 has invested heavily in building frameworks and structures (scoring 3.0–3.8 across pillars), yet struggles to translate these into measurable outcomes and sustained performance improvements. This "strategy-execution gap" is the defining strategic challenge.

Our hypothesis is that test-1's strategic imperative is to become a high-performance government institution by: (1) closing the strategy-execution gap through rigorous performance management and accountable leadership; (2) accelerating digital and data capabilities to drive efficiency and insight; (3) positioning as a regional benchmark by adopting international best practices; and (4) building organizational resilience through talent, culture, and risk management investments.

Success requires a 3-year transformation agenda organized around these four strategic pillars, with clear milestones, dedicated resources, and a performance culture that rewards results over activity.

Document Title: Cultural Assets Group — Corporate Strategy Plan 2024–2028 Classification: Confidential — Board Approved Version: 3.2 Final Date: January 15, 2024 Prepared by: Office of the Group CEO & Group Strategy DivisionApproved by: CAG Board of Directors — Resolution #BD-2024-003 (January 12, 2024) Format: PDF (48 pages)



TABLE OF CONTENTS

Chairman's Foreword

Group CEO's Strategic Letter

Who We Are — Mission, Vision & Values

Our Theory of Value Creation (Parenting Purpose)

Strategic Context & Environmental Scan

Group Strategic Pillars 2024–2028

Portfolio Strategy & Subsidiary Mandates

Financial Ambition & Capital Allocation Framework

Governance of Strategy Execution

Key Risks to Strategy

Appendices



1. CHAIRMAN'S FOREWORD

The Cultural Assets Group stands at an inflection point. Over the past decade, we have assembled a portfolio of six distinctive subsidiaries operating across the cultural economy — spanning heritage tourism, live entertainment, digital content, arts education, cultural real estate development, and creative services. Each subsidiary was acquired or incubated because of its intrinsic connection to culture as an asset class.

As I reflect on our journey, I am proud of what we have built but clear-eyed about what lies ahead. The global cultural economy is projected to reach USD 8.2 trillion by 2028 (UNESCO/Oxford Economics, 2023). Yet this growth will not be evenly distributed. It will accrue to organizations that can operate at the intersection of authenticity, technology, and scale — precisely where CAG is positioned.

This strategy document represents the Board's consensus on where we are headed and how we will get there. It is the product of six months of deliberation, subsidiary consultations, external advisory input, and rigorous financial modeling.

Sheikh Ahmed Al-Farsi Chairman, CAG Board of Directors



2. GROUP CEO'S STRATEGIC LETTER

To our Board, leadership teams, and stakeholders:

Our first strategic cycle (2019–2023) was defined by portfolio assembly. We acquired four subsidiaries, incubated two, and established the holding company's central functions. We achieved consolidated revenue of SAR 2.1 billion in FY2023, up from SAR 680 million in FY2019 — a CAGR of 32.6%.

Our second strategic cycle (2024–2028) must be defined by portfolio optimization and value multiplication. We must shift from "collection" to "connection" — unlocking the synergies between our subsidiaries that justified their acquisition in the first place.

Three convictions underpin this strategy:

Culture is the new infrastructure. Governments and consumers are investing in cultural experiences at unprecedented rates. Our subsidiaries sit on irreplaceable cultural assets.

The holding company must earn its right to exist. Every central function, every governance mechanism, every capital allocation decision must demonstrably add value that subsidiaries could not create alone.

Digital is not a pillar — it is the atmosphere. Every subsidiary strategy must be digitally native. We will invest SAR 400 million over five years in digital transformation across the group.

Nora Al-Rashid Group CEO, Cultural Assets Group



3. WHO WE ARE — MISSION, VISION & VALUES

3.1 Mission Statement

"To preserve, activate, and scale cultural assets for the enrichment of communities and the creation of sustainable economic value."

3.2 Vision Statement

"By 2028, CAG will be the Middle East and North Africa's leading cultural economy group — recognized for the authenticity of our cultural offerings, the excellence of our operations, and the impact of our investments on communities and stakeholders."

3.3 Core Values

Value

Definition

Behavioral Anchor

Authenticity

We honor the integrity of cultural assets and never compromise heritage for short-term gain

Every product/experience must pass the "Cultural Integrity Review"

Excellence

We pursue operational and creative excellence in everything we do

Zero tolerance for mediocrity; continuous improvement embedded in KPIs

Stewardship

We are custodians, not owners, of cultural assets — we hold them in trust for future generations

Long-term value creation over short-term extraction

Collaboration

We believe the group is greater than the sum of its parts

Cross-subsidiary projects are rewarded; silos are actively dismantled

Courage

We take bold, calculated bets on the future of culture

Innovation budget ring-fenced; failure-tolerant experimentation encouraged

3.4 Strategic Identity Summary

CAG is a strategic holding company (not a financial holding or passive investor). We actively shape subsidiary strategies, allocate capital with conviction, provide shared services where scale advantages exist, and intervene when subsidiaries underperform. Our parenting style is best described as "Strategic Architect" — we set the blueprint, resource the build, and monitor progress, but we empower subsidiary CEOs to lead execution.



4. OUR THEORY OF VALUE CREATION (PARENTING PURPOSE)

4.1 The Parenting Advantage Framework

CAG creates value for its subsidiaries through five mechanisms:

#

Value Creation Mechanism

Description

Example

1

Capital Allocation

Centralized capital allocation enables investment in highest-return opportunities across the portfolio, rather than each subsidiary self-funding

SAR 120M redirected from Subsidiary 4 (mature, cash-generative) to Subsidiary 2 (high-growth, capital-hungry) in 2023

2

Talent & Leadership Development

Group-wide talent pool, leadership rotation program, and centralized executive recruitment

Group CHRO manages top-50 leadership pipeline; 3 subsidiary CEOs rotated in 2022–2023

3

Shared Services & Scale Economies

Centralized procurement, finance, legal, IT infrastructure, and marketing analytics

Group procurement saved SAR 45M in FY2023 through consolidated vendor contracts

4

Brand & Reputation Halo

The CAG brand provides credibility, government access, and partnership leverage that individual subsidiaries could not achieve alone

CAG brand enabled Subsidiary 1 to secure a 25-year government concession valued at SAR 800M

5

Strategic Synergy Orchestration

Active identification and execution of cross-subsidiary revenue and cost synergies

"Cultural Passport" product (cross-selling across Subsidiaries 1, 2, and 5) generated SAR 28M incremental revenue in FY2023

4.2 Corporate-Level Strategy

CAG's corporate-level strategy is a Related-Linked Diversification strategy. Our subsidiaries are linked by:

A common focus on cultural assets as the core resource

Shared customer segments (cultural tourists, experience seekers, government/institutional buyers)

Complementary capabilities (content creation, venue management, digital distribution, education)

Geographic overlap (primarily MENA, with selective international expansion)

We explicitly reject unrelated diversification. Any future acquisition or incubation must pass the "Cultural Nexus Test": Does this entity's core business fundamentally depend on, or contribute to, the cultural economy?



5. STRATEGIC CONTEXT & ENVIRONMENTAL SCAN

5.1 Macro-Environmental Analysis (PESTEL)

Factor

Key Trends

Implication for CAG

Time Horizon

Political

Saudi Vision 2030 allocating SAR 50B+ to culture & entertainment; UAE cultural investment accelerating; Egypt cultural heritage monetization

Massive tailwind; government as customer, partner, and regulator simultaneously

Economic

Favorable demand environment; cost pressures easing

Social

Youth demographic bulge (65% under 35 in KSA); rising demand for experiential consumption; cultural identity as social currency

Core demand driver; product design must be youth-centric and Instagram-worthy

Structural

Opportunity and threat; must invest or be disrupted

Environmental

Must integrate sustainability into operations; potential competitive differentiator

2024–2028

Legal

Compliance investment required; IP protection critical for content subsidiaries

2024–2026

5.2 Industry Analysis — Cultural Economy Value Chain

The cultural economy value chain consists of four layers:

Cultural Asset Origination — Heritage sites, artistic creation, IP development

Cultural Asset Activation — Experiences, events, exhibitions, education

Cultural Asset Distribution — Digital platforms, media, licensing, merchandising

Cultural Asset Monetization — Ticketing, sponsorship, real estate, government contracts

CAG's portfolio spans all four layers, which is a distinctive competitive advantage. Most competitors operate in one or two layers.

5.4 SWOT Summary (Pre-Assessment — CEO's Perspective)



Positive

Negative

Internal

Strengths: Unique portfolio spanning full cultural value chain; strong government relationships; SAR 2.1B revenue base; talented subsidiary CEOs

Weaknesses: Synergies underexploited; digital maturity uneven across subsidiaries; holding company overhead questioned by some board members; financial reporting not yet fully consolidated in real-time

External

Opportunities: Vision 2030 cultural investment wave; digital/AI transformation of cultural experiences; international expansion (Egypt, Morocco, Turkey); "Cultural Passport" product scaling

Threats: Government entities competing directly; talent war for creative/tech professionals; regulatory uncertainty in new markets; economic downturn reducing discretionary cultural spending

Document Title: Cultural Assets Group — Corporate Strategy Plan 2024–2028 Classification: Confidential — Board Approved Version: 3.2 Final Date: January 15, 2024 Prepared by: Office of the Group CEO & Group Strategy DivisionApproved by: CAG Board of Directors — Resolution #BD-2024-003 (January 12, 2024) Format: PDF (48 pages)



TABLE OF CONTENTS

Chairman's Foreword

Group CEO's Strategic Letter

Who We Are — Mission, Vision & Values

Our Theory of Value Creation (Parenting Purpose)

Strategic Context & Environmental Scan

Group Strategic Pillars 2024–2028

Portfolio Strategy & Subsidiary Mandates

Financial Ambition & Capital Allocation Framework

Governance of Strategy Execution

Key Risks to Strategy

Appendices



1. CHAIRMAN'S FOREWORD

The Cultural Assets Group stands at an inflection point. Over the past decade, we have assembled a portfolio of six distinctive subsidiaries operating across the cultural economy — spanning heritage tourism, live entertainment, digital content, arts education, cultural real estate development, and creative services. Each subsidiary was acquired or incubated because of its intrinsic connection to culture as an asset class.

As I reflect on our journey, I am proud of what we have built but clear-eyed about what lies ahead. The global cultural economy is projected to reach USD 8.2 trillion by 2028 (UNESCO/Oxford Economics, 2023). Yet this growth will not be evenly distributed. It will accrue to organizations that can operate at the intersection of authenticity, technology, and scale — precisely where CAG is positioned.

This strategy document represents the Board's consensus on where we are headed and how we will get there. It is the product of six months of deliberation, subsidiary consultations, external advisory input, and rigorous financial modeling.

Sheikh Ahmed Al-Farsi Chairman, CAG Board of Directors



2. GROUP CEO'S STRATEGIC LETTER

To our Board, leadership teams, and stakeholders:

Our first strategic cycle (2019–2023) was defined by portfolio assembly. We acquired four subsidiaries, incubated two, and established the holding company's central functions. We achieved consolidated revenue of SAR 2.1 billion in FY2023, up from SAR 680 million in FY2019 — a CAGR of 32.6%.

Our second strategic cycle (2024–2028) must be defined by portfolio optimization and value multiplication. We must shift from "collection" to "connection" — unlocking the synergies between our subsidiaries that justified their acquisition in the first place.

Three convictions underpin this strategy:

Culture is the new infrastructure. Governments and consumers are investing in cultural experiences at unprecedented rates. Our subsidiaries sit on irreplaceable cultural assets.

The holding company must earn its right to exist. Every central function, every governance mechanism, every capital allocation decision must demonstrably add value that subsidiaries could not create alone.

Digital is not a pillar — it is the atmosphere. Every subsidiary strategy must be digitally native. We will invest SAR 400 million over five years in digital transformation across the group.

Nora Al-Rashid Group CEO, Cultural Assets Group



3. WHO WE ARE — MISSION, VISION & VALUES

3.1 Mission Statement

"To preserve, activate, and scale cultural assets for the enrichment of communities and the creation of sustainable economic value."

3.2 Vision Statement

"By 2028, CAG will be the Middle East and North Africa's leading cultural economy group — recognized for the authenticity of our cultural offerings, the excellence of our operations, and the impact of our investments on communities and stakeholders."

3.3 Core Values

Value

Definition

Behavioral Anchor

Authenticity

We honor the integrity of cultural assets and never compromise heritage for short-term gain

Every product/experience must pass the "Cultural Integrity Review"

Excellence

We pursue operational and creative excellence in everything we do

Zero tolerance for mediocrity; continuous improvement embedded in KPIs

Stewardship

We are custodians, not owners, of cultural assets — we hold them in trust for future generations

Long-term value creation over short-term extraction

Collaboration

We believe the group is greater than the sum of its parts

Cross-subsidiary projects are rewarded; silos are actively dismantled

Courage

We take bold, calculated bets on the future of culture

Innovation budget ring-fenced; failure-tolerant experimentation encouraged

3.4 Strategic Identity Summary

CAG is a strategic holding company (not a financial holding or passive investor). We actively shape subsidiary strategies, allocate capital with conviction, provide shared services where scale advantages exist, and intervene when subsidiaries underperform. Our parenting style is best described as "Strategic Architect" — we set the blueprint, resource the build, and monitor progress, but we empower subsidiary CEOs to lead execution.



4. OUR THEORY OF VALUE CREATION (PARENTING PURPOSE)

4.1 The Parenting Advantage Framework

CAG creates value for its subsidiaries through five mechanisms:

#

Value Creation Mechanism

Description

Example

1

Capital Allocation

Centralized capital allocation enables investment in highest-return opportunities across the portfolio, rather than each subsidiary self-funding

SAR 120M redirected from Subsidiary 4 (mature, cash-generative) to Subsidiary 2 (high-growth, capital-hungry) in 2023

2

Talent & Leadership Development

Group-wide talent pool, leadership rotation program, and centralized executive recruitment

Group CHRO manages top-50 leadership pipeline; 3 subsidiary CEOs rotated in 2022–2023

3

Shared Services & Scale Economies

Centralized procurement, finance, legal, IT infrastructure, and marketing analytics

Group procurement saved SAR 45M in FY2023 through consolidated vendor contracts

4

Brand & Reputation Halo

The CAG brand provides credibility, government access, and partnership leverage that individual subsidiaries could not achieve alone

CAG brand enabled Subsidiary 1 to secure a 25-year government concession valued at SAR 800M

5

Strategic Synergy Orchestration

Active identification and execution of cross-subsidiary revenue and cost synergies

"Cultural Passport" product (cross-selling across Subsidiaries 1, 2, and 5) generated SAR 28M incremental revenue in FY2023

4.2 Corporate-Level Strategy

CAG's corporate-level strategy is a Related-Linked Diversification strategy. Our subsidiaries are linked by:

A common focus on cultural assets as the core resource

Shared customer segments (cultural tourists, experience seekers, government/institutional buyers)

Complementary capabilities (content creation, venue management, digital distribution, education)

Geographic overlap (primarily MENA, with selective international expansion)

We explicitly reject unrelated diversification. Any future acquisition or incubation must pass the "Cultural Nexus Test": Does this entity's core business fundamentally depend on, or contribute to, the cultural economy?



5. STRATEGIC CONTEXT & ENVIRONMENTAL SCAN

5.1 Macro-Environmental Analysis (PESTEL)

Factor

Key Trends

Implication for CAG

Time Horizon

Core demand driver; product design must be youth-centric and Instagram-worthy

Opportunity and threat; must invest or be disrupted

2024–2028

Environmental

Must integrate sustainability into operations; potential competitive differentiator

2024–2028

Legal

Evolving IP frameworks in MENA; entertainment licensing reforms in KSA; data privacy regulations (PDPL)

Compliance investment required; IP protection critical for content subsidiaries

2024–2026

5.2 Industry Analysis — Cultural Economy Value Chain

The cultural economy value chain consists of four layers:

Cultural Asset Origination — Heritage sites, artistic creation, IP development

Cultural Asset Activation — Experiences, events, exhibitions, education

Cultural Asset Distribution — Digital platforms, media, licensing, merchandising

Cultural Asset Monetization — Ticketing, sponsorship, real estate, government contracts

CAG's portfolio spans all four layers, which is a distinctive competitive advantage. Most competitors operate in one or two layers.

1. CHAIRMAN'S FOREWORD

The Cultural Assets Group stands at an inflection point. Over the past decade, we have assembled a portfolio of six distinctive subsidiaries operating across the cultural economy — spanning heritage tourism, live entertainment, digital content, arts education, cultural real estate development, and creative services. Each subsidiary was acquired or incubated because of its intrinsic connection to culture as an asset class.

As I reflect on our journey, I am proud of what we have built but clear-eyed about what lies ahead. The global cultural economy is projected to reach USD 8.2 trillion by 2028 (UNESCO/Oxford Economics, 2023). Yet this growth will not be evenly distributed. It will accrue to organizations that can operate at the intersection of authenticity, technology, and scale — precisely where CAG is positioned.

This strategy document represents the Board's consensus on where we are headed and how we will get there. It is the product of six months of deliberation, subsidiary consultations, external advisory input, and rigorous financial modeling.

Sheikh Ahmed Al-Farsi Chairman, CAG Board of Directors



2. GROUP CEO'S STRATEGIC LETTER

To our Board, leadership teams, and stakeholders:

Our first strategic cycle (2019–2023) was defined by portfolio assembly. We acquired four subsidiaries, incubated two, and established the holding company's central functions. We achieved consolidated revenue of SAR 2.1 billion in FY2023, up from SAR 680 million in FY2019 — a CAGR of 32.6%.

Our second strategic cycle (2024–2028) must be defined by portfolio optimization and value multiplication. We must shift from "collection" to "connection" — unlocking the synergies between our subsidiaries that justified their acquisition in the first place.

Three convictions underpin this strategy:

Culture is the new infrastructure. Governments and consumers are investing in cultural experiences at unprecedented rates. Our subsidiaries sit on irreplaceable cultural assets.

The holding company must earn its right to exist. Every central function, every governance mechanism, every capital allocation decision must demonstrably add value that subsidiaries could not create alone.

Digital is not a pillar — it is the atmosphere. Every subsidiary strategy must be digitally native. We will invest SAR 400 million over five years in digital transformation across the group.

Nora Al-Rashid Group CEO, Cultural Assets Group



3. WHO WE ARE — MISSION, VISION & VALUES

3.1 Mission Statement

"To preserve, activate, and scale cultural assets for the enrichment of communities and the creation of sustainable economic value."

3.2 Vision Statement

"By 2028, CAG will be the Middle East and North Africa's leading cultural economy group — recognized for the authenticity of our cultural offerings, the excellence of our operations, and the impact of our investments on communities and stakeholders."

3.3 Core Values

Value

Definition

Behavioral Anchor

Authenticity

We honor the integrity of cultural assets and never compromise heritage for short-term gain

Every product/experience must pass the "Cultural Integrity Review"

Excellence

We pursue operational and creative excellence in everything we do

Zero tolerance for mediocrity; continuous improvement embedded in KPIs

Stewardship

We are custodians, not owners, of cultural assets — we hold them in trust for future generations

Long-term value creation over short-term extraction

Collaboration

We believe the group is greater than the sum of its parts

Cross-subsidiary projects are rewarded; silos are actively dismantled

Courage

We take bold, calculated bets on the future of culture

Innovation budget ring-fenced; failure-tolerant experimentation encouraged

3.4 Strategic Identity Summary

CAG is a strategic holding company (not a financial holding or passive investor). We actively shape subsidiary strategies, allocate capital with conviction, provide shared services where scale advantages exist, and intervene when subsidiaries underperform. Our parenting style is best described as "Strategic Architect" — we set the blueprint, resource the build, and monitor progress, but we empower subsidiary CEOs to lead execution.



4. OUR THEORY OF VALUE CREATION (PARENTING PURPOSE)

4.1 The Parenting Advantage Framework

CAG creates value for its subsidiaries through five mechanisms:

#

Value Creation Mechanism

Description

Example

1

Capital Allocation

Centralized capital allocation enables investment in highest-return opportunities across the portfolio, rather than each subsidiary self-funding

SAR 120M redirected from Subsidiary 4 (mature, cash-generative) to Subsidiary 2 (high-growth, capital-hungry) in 2023

2

Talent & Leadership Development

Group-wide talent pool, leadership rotation program, and centralized executive recruitment

Group CHRO manages top-50 leadership pipeline; 3 subsidiary CEOs rotated in 2022–2023

3

Shared Services & Scale Economies

Centralized procurement, finance, legal, IT infrastructure, and marketing analytics

Group procurement saved SAR 45M in FY2023 through consolidated vendor contracts

4

Brand & Reputation Halo

The CAG brand provides credibility, government access, and partnership leverage that individual subsidiaries could not achieve alone

CAG brand enabled Subsidiary 1 to secure a 25-year government concession valued at SAR 800M

5

Strategic Synergy Orchestration

Active identification and execution of cross-subsidiary revenue and cost synergies

"Cultural Passport" product (cross-selling across Subsidiaries 1, 2, and 5) generated SAR 28M incremental revenue in FY2023

4.2 Corporate-Level Strategy

CAG's corporate-level strategy is a Related-Linked Diversification strategy. Our subsidiaries are linked by:

A common focus on cultural assets as the core resource

Shared customer segments (cultural tourists, experience seekers, government/institutional buyers)

Complementary capabilities (content creation, venue management, digital distribution, education)

Geographic overlap (primarily MENA, with selective international expansion)

We explicitly reject unrelated diversification. Any future acquisition or incubation must pass the "Cultural Nexus Test": Does this entity's core business fundamentally depend on, or contribute to, the cultural economy?

Document Title: Cultural Assets Group — Corporate Strategy Plan 2024–2028 Classification: Confidential — Board Approved Version: 3.2 Final Date: January 15, 2024 Prepared by: Office of the Group CEO & Group Strategy DivisionApproved by: CAG Board of Directors — Resolution #BD-2024-003 (January 12, 2024) Format: PDF (48 pages)



TABLE OF CONTENTS

Chairman's Foreword

Group CEO's Strategic Letter

Who We Are — Mission, Vision & Values

Our Theory of Value Creation (Parenting Purpose)

Strategic Context & Environmental Scan

Group Strategic Pillars 2024–2028

Portfolio Strategy & Subsidiary Mandates

Financial Ambition & Capital Allocation Framework

Governance of Strategy Execution

Key Risks to Strategy

Appendices



1. CHAIRMAN'S FOREWORD

The Cultural Assets Group stands at an inflection point. Over the past decade, we have assembled a portfolio of six distinctive subsidiaries operating across the cultural economy — spanning heritage tourism, live entertainment, digital content, arts education, cultural real estate development, and creative services. Each subsidiary was acquired or incubated because of its intrinsic connection to culture as an asset class.

As I reflect on our journey, I am proud of what we have built but clear-eyed about what lies ahead. The global cultural economy is projected to reach USD 8.2 trillion by 2028 (UNESCO/Oxford Economics, 2023). Yet this growth will not be evenly distributed. It will accrue to organizations that can operate at the intersection of authenticity, technology, and scale — precisely where CAG is positioned.

This strategy document represents the Board's consensus on where we are headed and how we will get there. It is the product of six months of deliberation, subsidiary consultations, external advisory input, and rigorous financial modeling.

Sheikh Ahmed Al-Farsi Chairman, CAG Board of Directors



2. GROUP CEO'S STRATEGIC LETTER

To our Board, leadership teams, and stakeholders:

Our first strategic cycle (2019–2023) was defined by portfolio assembly. We acquired four subsidiaries, incubated two, and established the holding company's central functions. We achieved consolidated revenue of SAR 2.1 billion in FY2023, up from SAR 680 million in FY2019 — a CAGR of 32.6%.

Our second strategic cycle (2024–2028) must be defined by portfolio optimization and value multiplication. We must shift from "collection" to "connection" — unlocking the synergies between our subsidiaries that justified their acquisition in the first place.

Three convictions underpin this strategy:

Culture is the new infrastructure. Governments and consumers are investing in cultural experiences at unprecedented rates. Our subsidiaries sit on irreplaceable cultural assets.

The holding company must earn its right to exist. Every central function, every governance mechanism, every capital allocation decision must demonstrably add value that subsidiaries could not create alone.

Digital is not a pillar — it is the atmosphere. Every subsidiary strategy must be digitally native. We will invest SAR 400 million over five years in digital transformation across the group.

Nora Al-Rashid Group CEO, Cultural Assets Group



3. WHO WE ARE — MISSION, VISION & VALUES

3.1 Mission Statement

"To preserve, activate, and scale cultural assets for the enrichment of communities and the creation of sustainable economic value."

3.2 Vision Statement

"By 2028, CAG will be the Middle East and North Africa's leading cultural economy group — recognized for the authenticity of our cultural offerings, the excellence of our operations, and the impact of our investments on communities and stakeholders."

3.3 Core Values

Value

Definition

Behavioral Anchor

Authenticity

We honor the integrity of cultural assets and never compromise heritage for short-term gain

Every product/experience must pass the "Cultural Integrity Review"

Excellence

We pursue operational and creative excellence in everything we do

Zero tolerance for mediocrity; continuous improvement embedded in KPIs

Stewardship

We are custodians, not owners, of cultural assets — we hold them in trust for future generations

Long-term value creation over short-term extraction

Collaboration

We believe the group is greater than the sum of its parts

Cross-subsidiary projects are rewarded; silos are actively dismantled

Courage

We take bold, calculated bets on the future of culture

Innovation budget ring-fenced; failure-tolerant experimentation encouraged

3.4 Strategic Identity Summary

CAG is a strategic holding company (not a financial holding or passive investor). We actively shape subsidiary strategies, allocate capital with conviction, provide shared services where scale advantages exist, and intervene when subsidiaries underperform. Our parenting style is best described as "Strategic Architect" — we set the blueprint, resource the build, and monitor progress, but we empower subsidiary CEOs to lead execution.



4. OUR THEORY OF VALUE CREATION (PARENTING PURPOSE)

4.1 The Parenting Advantage Framework

CAG creates value for its subsidiaries through five mechanisms:

#

Value Creation Mechanism

Description

Example

1

Capital Allocation

Centralized capital allocation enables investment in highest-return opportunities across the portfolio, rather than each subsidiary self-funding

SAR 120M redirected from Subsidiary 4 (mature, cash-generative) to Subsidiary 2 (high-growth, capital-hungry) in 2023

2

Talent & Leadership Development

Group-wide talent pool, leadership rotation program, and centralized executive recruitment

Group CHRO manages top-50 leadership pipeline; 3 subsidiary CEOs rotated in 2022–2023

3

Shared Services & Scale Economies

Centralized procurement, finance, legal, IT infrastructure, and marketing analytics

Group procurement saved SAR 45M in FY2023 through consolidated vendor contracts

4

Brand & Reputation Halo

The CAG brand provides credibility, government access, and partnership leverage that individual subsidiaries could not achieve alone

CAG brand enabled Subsidiary 1 to secure a 25-year government concession valued at SAR 800M

5

Strategic Synergy Orchestration

Active identification and execution of cross-subsidiary revenue and cost synergies

"Cultural Passport" product (cross-selling across Subsidiaries 1, 2, and 5) generated SAR 28M incremental revenue in FY2023

4.2 Corporate-Level Strategy

CAG's corporate-level strategy is a Related-Linked Diversification strategy. Our subsidiaries are linked by:

A common focus on cultural assets as the core resource

Shared customer segments (cultural tourists, experience seekers, government/institutional buyers)

Complementary capabilities (content creation, venue management, digital distribution, education)

Geographic overlap (primarily MENA, with selective international expansion)

We explicitly reject unrelated diversification. Any future acquisition or incubation must pass the "Cultural Nexus Test": Does this entity's core business fundamentally depend on, or contribute to, the cultural economy?

5.2 Industry Analysis — Cultural Economy Value Chain

The cultural economy value chain consists of four layers:

Cultural Asset Origination — Heritage sites, artistic creation, IP development

Cultural Asset Activation — Experiences, events, exhibitions, education

Cultural Asset Distribution — Digital platforms, media, licensing, merchandising

Cultural Asset Monetization — Ticketing, sponsorship, real estate, government contracts

CAG's portfolio spans all four layers, which is a distinctive competitive advantage. Most competitors operate in one or two layers.

P1.name: Strategic Identity & Vision
P1.description: What is the entity's reason for being and where is it headed?

elements.name: Mission & Vision Clarity
elements.aiAnswer: CAG Holding GmbH does not have a publicly articulated formal mission or vision statement at the holding level. The entity does not maintain its own website **[<333,019dc4a5-f173-7abf-9b58-92a48efdd07c>]**. The closest approximation to a mission is found on LinkedIn: 'We sustain and develop industrial companies' with a description that the holding 'holds international investments that use glass, aluminium and biomass to create sustainable products and services of lasting value and great customer benefit' **[<302,019dc4a5-98b2-74c4-a9d9-59e22a0e2cc8>, <334,019dc4a5-f174-7ee0-9a3a-dcecee01f4c0>, <337,019dc4a5-f177-7fd7-820b-aadaedbaea86>]**. This implies a purpose centered on industrial sustainability and value creation through materials (glass, aluminium, biomass), but it lacks the specificity, differentiation, and inspirational quality expected of a formal mission statement. No time-bound vision was identified. Subsidiary-level statements exist — PREFA references CAG's responsibility ethos **[<363,019dc4a6-0c79-7fa2-965c-2a12b31b8c9c>]**, and Stoelzle articulates a partner-of-choice aspiration **[<338,019dc4a5-f178-70ba-9291-2a7291d30b9d>]** — but no unified holding-level vision cascades across the group. The holding's deliberate discretion ('Die CAG Holding verzichtet sogar darauf, eine eigene Website zu betreiben' — CAG Holding even refrains from operating its own website) **[<333,019dc4a5-f173-7abf-9b58-92a48efdd07c>]** suggests a strategic choice of privacy over public strategic communication, which is consistent with family-owned industrial holdings but creates a significant gap in strategic identity clarity.
elements.evidenceQuote: The CAG Holding is a family-owned holding company that holds international investments that use glass, aluminium and biomass to create sustainable products and services of lasting value and great customer benefit. **[<302,019dc4a5-98b2-74c4-a9d9-59e22a0e2cc8>, <334,019dc4a5-f174-7ee0-9a3a-dcecee01f4c0>, <337,019dc4a5-f177-7fd7-820b-aadaedbaea86>]**
elements.scoreRationale: No formal mission or vision statement was found in the document collection. The RAG tool returned only Dubai Courts Family Guidance and Reconciliation Section documents [1-1 through 6-50], which are entirely unrelated to CAG Holding GmbH. Web search revealed that CAG Holding's LinkedIn profile states: 'We sustain and develop industrial companies' and describes the holding as 'a family-owned holding company that holds international investments that use glass, aluminium and biomass to create sustainable products and services of lasting value and great customer benefit' **[<302,019dc4a5-98b2-74c4-a9d9-59e22a0e2cc8>, <334,019dc4a5-f174-7ee0-9a3a-dcecee01f4c0>, <337,019dc4a5-f177-7fd7-820b-aadaedbaea86>]**. This serves as a de facto mission but is not a formally articulated, differentiated mission statement. No time-bound vision statement was found. The subsidiary PREFA references CAG values on its website: 'We at CAG take our responsibility seriously – for ourselves, for our company and the regions in which we operate' **[<363,019dc4a6-0c79-7fa2-965c-2a12b31b8c9c>]**, and Stoelzle references 'Our aim is to be the first choice partner for both our customers and our employees' **[<338,019dc4a5-f178-70ba-9291-2a7291d30b9d>]**, but these are subsidiary-level, not holding-level vision statements. The absence of a dedicated CAG Holding website **[<333,019dc4a5-f173-7abf-9b58-92a48efdd07c>]** further limits visibility of any formal mission/vision. Score of 2 reflects the existence of an implicit purpose statement but no formally articulated, differentiated, or time-bound mission and vision at the holding level.
elements.dataGap: No formal holding-level mission statement, vision statement, or strategic identity document was found in the document collection or publicly available sources. The LinkedIn description serves as the only proxy.

elements.name: Strategic Intent
elements.aiAnswer: No formal 3-5 year strategic intent or ambition document exists for CAG Holding at the holding level. The entity operates as a private, family-owned industrial holding with approximately 9,000-9,800 employees across 40+ production sites worldwide **[<334,019dc4a5-f174-7ee0-9a3a-dcecee01f4c0>, <340,019dc4a5-f17a-752e-9935-6b5b2cae2289>]**. Evidence of strategic activity includes the recent acquisition of INDAT GmbH to gain 'specialists with extensive know-how' in 'special machine construction, robotics, model and mould construction as well as CNC production' **[<373,019dc4a6-329e-76a8-bbcc-2cf727ca43c8>]**. This suggests a strategy of vertical integration and capability building within the aluminium value chain. At the subsidiary level, Stoelzle Glass Group has a Sustainability Roadmap 2025 with SBTi-approved targets **[<386,019dc4a6-2c5a-7486-bb76-0aa539672037>, <389,019dc4a6-2c5d-7da1-a47b-521f4f5147b8>]**, and PREFA emphasizes sustainability with 86.6% recycled content in small roof formats **[<364,019dc4a6-0c7a-7659-9018-91da762de7b7>]**. However, these subsidiary strategies do not roll up into a visible holding-level strategic framework. No SMART objectives, ranked priorities, or time-bound ambitions were identified for the holding entity itself.
elements.evidenceQuote: INDAT has established itself over the years as a reliable partner with a high level of innovative strength - we want to preserve and further develop this expertise **[<373,019dc4a6-329e-76a8-bbcc-2cf727ca43c8>]**
elements.scoreRationale: No 3-5 year strategic plan, SMART objectives, or ranked strategic priorities were found for CAG Holding in either the document collection or public sources. The RAG tool returned no relevant CAG Holding documents [1-1 through 6-50 were all Dubai Courts documents]. Web search revealed evidence of recent portfolio expansion through the acquisition of INDAT GmbH **[<373,019dc4a6-329e-76a8-bbcc-2cf727ca43c8>]**, with Dr. Cornelius Grupp stating: 'INDAT has established itself over the years as a reliable partner with a high level of innovative strength - we want to preserve and further develop this expertise' **[<373,019dc4a6-329e-76a8-bbcc-2cf727ca43c8>]**. This suggests an acquisitive growth intent but does not constitute a formal strategic plan. Subsidiary-level strategies exist — Stoelzle has a 'Sustainability Strategy 2025' with 'a clear focus set on energy efficiency, decarbonization and recycling management' **[<386,019dc4a6-2c5a-7486-bb76-0aa539672037>]** and SBTi-approved targets to 'reduce absolute GHG emissions (Scope 1 and 2) by 50% by 2030' **[<387,019dc4a6-2c5b-7ab1-b35b-25bb8c70f29a>]**. However, no consolidated holding-level strategic intent document was identified. Score of 1 reflects the complete absence of a documented, SMART, time-bound strategic intent at the holding level.
elements.dataGap: No holding-level strategic plan, 3-5 year ambition document, SMART objectives, or ranked strategic priorities were found. Only subsidiary-level strategies (Stoelzle Sustainability Strategy 2025) and ad hoc acquisition announcements exist.

elements.name: Value Proposition
elements.aiAnswer: CAG Holding's value proposition is implicitly communicated through its subsidiaries rather than formally articulated at the holding level. The core value creation logic appears to center on: (1) sustainable industrial manufacturing using glass, aluminium, and biomass **[<302,019dc4a5-98b2-74c4-a9d9-59e22a0e2cc8>, <334,019dc4a5-f174-7ee0-9a3a-dcecee01f4c0>]**; (2) long-term ownership stability as a family-owned entity providing patient capital **[<333,019dc4a5-f173-7abf-9b58-92a48efdd07c>, <339,019dc4a5-f179-7b28-83ca-01f508bbd467>]**; (3) synergy creation across related industrial companies — Stoelzle notes 'The firm integration within the CAG-Holding creates key synergies with Stoelzle's partner companies' **[<338,019dc4a5-f178-70ba-9291-2a7291d30b9d>]**; and (4) regional responsibility — 'We don't just work to ensure we continuously improve as a company: we also want to improve living standards in the regions in which we operate' **[<363,019dc4a6-0c79-7fa2-965c-2a12b31b8c9c>]**. TUBEX explicitly states that 'Collaboration with the other companies in CAG Holding, which is wholly owned by the industrialist Cornelius Alexander Grupp, is an invaluable market advantage for us' **[<320,019dc4a5-c631-7f69-bf01-597556f10ce6>]**. However, this value proposition is not consolidated, formally communicated, or differentiated against comparable industrial holdings.
elements.evidenceQuote: Collaboration with the other companies in CAG Holding, which is wholly owned by the industrialist Cornelius Alexander Grupp, is an invaluable market advantage for us. **[<320,019dc4a5-c631-7f69-bf01-597556f10ce6>]**
elements.scoreRationale: CAG Holding's implicit value proposition can be inferred from its LinkedIn description and subsidiary communications but is not formally articulated as a differentiated holding-level value proposition. The LinkedIn profile states the holding creates 'sustainable products and services of lasting value and great customer benefit' through 'glass, aluminium and biomass' **[<302,019dc4a5-98b2-74c4-a9d9-59e22a0e2cc8>, <334,019dc4a5-f174-7ee0-9a3a-dcecee01f4c0>]**. Subsidiary-level value propositions are clearer: PREFA offers a 40-year guarantee on aluminium roofing products **[<366,019dc4a6-0c7c-7f64-a2df-5545e078e77b>]**, Stoelzle positions itself as 'the first choice partner' in glass packaging **[<338,019dc4a5-f178-70ba-9291-2a7291d30b9d>]**, and Neuman Aluminium leverages the group's scale as 'an invaluable advantage' in the market **[<340,019dc4a5-f17a-752e-9935-6b5b2cae2289>]**. The PREFA website explicitly states: 'We at CAG take our responsibility seriously – for ourselves, for our company and the regions in which we operate' **[<363,019dc4a6-0c79-7fa2-965c-2a12b31b8c9c>]**. However, the holding-level value proposition to stakeholders (shareholders, subsidiaries, employees) is not explicitly differentiated from other industrial holding companies. Score of 2 reflects the existence of an implicit value proposition through subsidiary communications but no formally articulated, differentiated holding-level value proposition.
elements.dataGap: No formal holding-level value proposition document, stakeholder value framework, or competitive positioning statement was found. Value proposition is inferred from subsidiary communications only.

elements.name: Strategic Coherence
elements.aiAnswer: CAG Holding demonstrates implicit thematic coherence across its portfolio — all subsidiaries operate in sustainable materials and energy sectors (aluminium, glass, biomass) **[<302,019dc4a5-98b2-74c4-a9d9-59e22a0e2cc8>, <334,019dc4a5-f174-7ee0-9a3a-dcecee01f4c0>]**. The holding's LinkedIn tagline 'We sustain and develop industrial companies' **[<334,019dc4a5-f174-7ee0-9a3a-dcecee01f4c0>]** aligns with observable subsidiary activities: PREFA's 40-year guarantee and 86.6% recycled content **[<364,019dc4a6-0c7a-7659-9018-91da762de7b7>, <366,019dc4a6-0c7c-7f64-a2df-5545e078e77b>]**, Stoelzle's SBTi-approved 50% GHG reduction target by 2030 **[<387,019dc4a6-2c5b-7ab1-b35b-25bb8c70f29a>]**, TUBEX's circular economy initiatives **[<319,019dc4a5-c630-7ca0-913e-be38a0519033>, <320,019dc4a5-c631-7f69-bf01-597556f10ce6>]**, and Bioenergie Kärnten's green energy supply **[<392,019dc4a6-585e-751a-9f89-b79a4e3b25bb>]**. The INDAT acquisition suggests vertical integration logic within the aluminium segment **[<373,019dc4a6-329e-76a8-bbcc-2cf727ca43c8>]**. However, no formal strategic cascade document was found linking holding-level strategy to subsidiary-level execution. There is no evidence of shared performance frameworks, group-wide KPIs, or a formal portfolio strategy articulating how the glass, aluminium, and biomass segments create synergistic value. The holding's deliberate privacy posture **[<333,019dc4a5-f173-7abf-9b58-92a48efdd07c>]** may mean such documents exist internally but are not publicly available. The absence of a holding website and the reliance on subsidiary-level communications for strategic messaging creates a coherence gap in external perception.
elements.evidenceQuote: The firm integration within the CAG-Holding (located in Niederösterreich, Austria) creates key synergies with Stoelzle's partner companies. **[<338,019dc4a5-f178-70ba-9291-2a7291d30b9d>]**
elements.scoreRationale: Strategic coherence between the holding level and subsidiary level cannot be fully assessed due to the absence of a formal holding-level strategy document. However, observable coherence exists in the thematic alignment around sustainability and materials expertise. All major subsidiaries operate in materials manufacturing (aluminium: PREFA, Neuman Aluminium, TUBEX; glass: Stoelzle Glass Group, Stoelzle Lausitz; biomass energy: Bioenergie Kärnten) **[<302,019dc4a5-98b2-74c4-a9d9-59e22a0e2cc8>, <334,019dc4a5-f174-7ee0-9a3a-dcecee01f4c0>]**. Sustainability is a consistent theme: PREFA uses 86.6% recycled aluminium in small roof formats **[<364,019dc4a6-0c7a-7659-9018-91da762de7b7>]**, Stoelzle has SBTi-approved emissions targets **[<387,019dc4a6-2c5b-7ab1-b35b-25bb8c70f29a>, <389,019dc4a6-2c5d-7da1-a47b-521f4f5147b8>]**, and Bioenergie Kärnten supplies green heat and electricity **[<392,019dc4a6-585e-751a-9f89-b79a4e3b25bb>]**. The INDAT acquisition strengthens the aluminium value chain with machine construction and robotics capabilities **[<373,019dc4a6-329e-76a8-bbcc-2cf727ca43c8>]**. However, no formal strategic cascade from holding to subsidiary was identified, no evidence of shared KPIs or performance frameworks exists, and the relationship between the glass, aluminium, and biomass segments is not articulated in a coherent portfolio strategy. Score of 2 reflects thematic alignment but no documented strategic cascade.
elements.dataGap: No formal strategic cascade document, shared KPI framework, portfolio strategy, or holding-to-subsidiary alignment mechanism was found. Strategic coherence is inferred from thematic consistency across subsidiaries.

elements.name: Parenting Purpose
elements.aiAnswer: CAG Holding's parenting purpose is implicitly demonstrated through several mechanisms but not formally articulated in any identified document. Observable parenting activities include: (1) Linkage influence — cross-subsidiary synergies are referenced by Stoelzle **[<338,019dc4a5-f178-70ba-9291-2a7291d30b9d>]** and TUBEX **[<320,019dc4a5-c631-7f69-bf01-597556f10ce6>]**, and the INDAT acquisition explicitly leverages existing customer relationships with PREFA and Neuman Aluminium **[<373,019dc4a6-329e-76a8-bbcc-2cf727ca43c8>]**; (2) Central functions — shared energy infrastructure at the Marktl production site with a hydroelectric power plant serving CAG Holding production sites **[<364,019dc4a6-0c7a-7659-9018-91da762de7b7>]**; (3) Corporate development — active portfolio management through acquisitions (INDAT) to build capabilities in machine construction, robotics, and CNC production **[<373,019dc4a6-329e-76a8-bbcc-2cf727ca43c8>]**; (4) Stand-alone influence — long-term ownership stability as a family-owned entity providing patient capital and strategic continuity, with Dr. Cornelius Alexander Grupp as sole owner and managing director **[<333,019dc4a5-f173-7abf-9b58-92a48efdd07c>, <339,019dc4a5-f179-7b28-83ca-01f508bbd467>]**. The holding's deliberate discretion and absence of a website **[<333,019dc4a5-f173-7abf-9b58-92a48efdd07c>]** suggest these may exist internally but are not publicly communicated.
elements.evidenceQuote: Local companies in the group - including PREFA and Neuman Aluminium - were already customers of INDAT in the past. **[<373,019dc4a6-329e-76a8-bbcc-2cf727ca43c8>]**
elements.scoreRationale: CAG Holding's parenting purpose can be partially inferred but is not formally articulated. The holding is wholly owned by Dr. Cornelius Alexander Grupp **[<333,019dc4a5-f173-7abf-9b58-92a48efdd07c>, <339,019dc4a5-f179-7b28-83ca-01f508bbd467>]** and operates as a family-owned industrial holding with subsidiaries in aluminium (PREFA, Neuman Aluminium, TUBEX), glass (Stoelzle Glass Group, Stoelzle Lausitz), and biomass energy (Bioenergie Kärnten) **[<302,019dc4a5-98b2-74c4-a9d9-59e22a0e2cc8>, <334,019dc4a5-f174-7ee0-9a3a-dcecee01f4c0>]**. Evidence of parenting value includes: (1) synergy creation — 'The firm integration within the CAG-Holding creates key synergies with Stoelzle's partner companies' **[<338,019dc4a5-f178-70ba-9291-2a7291d30b9d>]**; (2) market advantage through group membership — TUBEX states collaboration with CAG companies is 'an invaluable market advantage' **[<320,019dc4a5-c631-7f69-bf01-597556f10ce6>]**; (3) shared infrastructure — 'a hydroelectric power plant now supplies 9.5% of the power consumed by the CAG Holding production sites in Marktl' **[<364,019dc4a6-0c7a-7659-9018-91da762de7b7>]**; (4) portfolio development through acquisitions — INDAT was acquired to add machine construction and robotics capabilities, with existing group companies (PREFA, Neuman Aluminium) already being INDAT customers **[<373,019dc4a6-329e-76a8-bbcc-2cf727ca43c8>]**. However, no formal parenting advantage framework (stand-alone influence, linkage influence, central functions, corporate development) was documented. The corporate-level strategy is not articulated. P2.name: Governance & Leadership
P2.description: How is the entity governed and led?

execSummary.aiDraft:
• CAG's board comprises 9 members with 3 independents (33%), 3 executives, 1 non-executive chairman, and 2 government representatives (MoC and PIF), which meets minimum Saudi CMA independence thresholds but falls short of best-practice majority-independence standards
• Four board committees are established — Audit & Risk, Nomination & Remuneration, Investment, and Strategy — however the Investment Committee is chaired by the Group CEO (Nora Al-Rashid), creating a potential conflict of interest where management chairs a board-level oversight committee
• The Group Executive Committee (GEC) includes six C-suite roles (CEO, CFO, COO, CHRO, CMO, CTO, CLO) reporting to the Group CEO, demonstrating a comprehensive functional leadership structure, but no evidence of succession planning, leadership development programs, or leadership performance evaluation frameworks exists in the documents
• The strategy document explicitly articulates a parenting philosophy — 'The holding company must earn its right to exist. Every central function, every governance mechanism, every capital allocation decision must demonstrably add value that subsidiaries could not create alone' — indicating a self-aware strategic guide parenting model
• The strategy was developed through 'six months of deliberation, subsidiary consultations, external advisory input, and rigorous financial modeling' and approved via Board Resolution #BD-2024-003, demonstrating structured strategic decision-making at the board level
• Holding company overhead grew from SAR 48M (FY2021) to SAR 78M (FY2023) with holding EBITDA of negative SAR 85M in FY2023, raising questions about whether the holding company cost structure is justified relative to value added
• No evidence was found in any document regarding board meeting frequency, delegation of authority frameworks, KPI cascading mechanisms, performance review cadence, or consequence management for underperformance
• A potential governance concern exists with Eng. Tariq Al-Harbi serving simultaneously as a board member and CEO of Subsidiary 6 (Cultural Real Estate), which could create conflicts when the board reviews subsidiary performance or capital allocation decisions

elements.name: Board Composition & Effectiveness
elements.aiAnswer:
• The board has 9 members: 1 Non-Executive Chairman (Sheikh Ahmed Al-Farsi), 3 Independent directors (Dr. Fatima Al-Dosari as Vice Chair, Dr. Sarah Al-Otaibi with academic background, James Richardson as international member), 3 Executive directors (Group CEO Nora Al-Rashid, Group CFO Khalid Al-Mutairi, and Eng. Tariq Al-Harbi who is CEO of Sub 6), and 2 Government Representatives (Mohammed Al-Qahtani from Ministry of Culture and Abdulaziz Al-Shehri from PIF)
• Independence ratio is 33% (3 of 9), which meets Saudi CMA minimum requirements but falls below the OECD-recommended practice of majority independence; executive representation at 33% is high for a holding company board
• Four board committees exist: Audit & Risk Committee (chaired by independent Dr. Al-Otaibi), Nomination & Remuneration Committee (chaired by independent Dr. Al-Dosari), Investment Committee (chaired by Group CEO Nora Al-Rashid — a governance concern as an executive chairs an oversight committee), and Strategy Committee (chaired by independent James Richardson)
• The board approved the 2024-2028 Corporate Strategy via Resolution #BD-2024-003 on January 12, 2024, demonstrating active strategic oversight
• No information is available on board meeting frequency, board evaluation processes, director skills matrix, term limits, or board training programs
• Gender diversity is present with at least 3 female members identified (Dr. Al-Dosari, Nora Al-Rashid, Dr. Al-Otaibi), representing approximately 33% female representation which is above the OECD 2024 average of 29%

elements.name: Parenting Style
elements.aiAnswer:
• The strategy document explicitly articulates a parenting philosophy through the Group CEO's statement: 'The holding company must earn its right to exist. Every central function, every governance mechanism, every capital allocation decision must demonstrably add value that subsidiaries could not create alone'
• The strategy includes a dedicated section on 'Our Theory of Value Creation (Parenting Purpose)' and 'Portfolio Strategy & Subsidiary Mandates,' indicating a deliberate and articulated parenting approach
• The second strategic cycle (2024-2028) is defined as 'portfolio optimization and value multiplication' with a shift from 'collection to connection — unlocking the synergies between our subsidiaries that justified their acquisition in the first place'
• The holding company incurs significant overhead: SAR 78M in holding company overhead plus SAR 28M in shared services costs (FY2023), with holding EBITDA at negative SAR 85M, suggesting a strategic guide model with active central functions rather than a passive financial holding
• The strategy document includes a 'Financial Ambition & Capital Allocation Framework' section, indicating centralized capital allocation — a hallmark of a strategic guide parenting style
• Eng. Tariq Al-Harbi (CEO of Sub 6) sits on the board, suggesting some subsidiaries have direct board-level representation while others may not, creating potential asymmetry in parent-subsidiary engagement
• No evidence of differentiated parenting approaches by subsidiary maturity (e.g., Digital Content at -5% EBITDA margin vs. Education at 28.1% EBITDA margin may require different oversight models)
elements.evidenceQuote: The holding company must earn its right to exist. Every central function, every governance mechanism, every capital allocation decision must demonstrably add value that subsidiaries could not create alone.
elements.sourceDocument: CAG CORPORATE STRATEGY DOCUMENT 2024.docx
elements.scoreRationale: CAG demonstrates a well-articulated parenting philosophy with explicit statements about value creation purpose, a dedicated theory of value creation section, and a clear strategic direction for portfolio optimization. The presence of centralized capital allocation, shared services, and a strategy that explicitly addresses the holding company's right to exist indicates a mature strategic guide model. The score is limited from 5 because there is no evidence of differentiated parenting by subsidiary maturity and the full parenting framework details were not available in the document excerpt.
elements.dataGap: Full content of 'Our Theory of Value Creation (Parenting Purpose)' section, differentiated parenting approaches by subsidiary maturity, subsidiary autonomy levels, and specific mechanisms for parent-subsidiary engagement (e.g., subsidiary board representation, reporting cadence)

P3.name: Financial Health & Performance
P3.description: How financially sound and performant is the entity?

execSummary.aiDraft:
• CAG achieved consolidated revenue of SAR 2.1 billion in FY2023, up from SAR 680 million in FY2019, representing a CAGR of 32.6% — an exceptional top-line growth trajectory driven by portfolio assembly and organic expansion across six subsidiaries
• Gross margin stabilized at 40.0% in FY2023 (vs. 41.2% in FY2021), while EBITDA grew from SAR 222M to SAR 426M (36.5% YoY) and net profit reached SAR 251M (43.4% YoY growth), demonstrating improving profitability; however, Adjusted EBITDA margin has remained flat at ~18.2% for three consecutive years
• Liquidity position is deteriorating with current ratio declining from 1.16x to 1.03x and quick ratio falling to 0.81x (below 1.0), while net debt has risen from SAR 410M to SAR 720M — signaling growing solvency pressure from aggressive capital deployment
• Free cash flow has been persistently negative (SAR -45M in FY2021 to SAR -129M in FY2023) driven by heavy capex of SAR 465M in FY2023 (22.1% of revenue), though operating cash flow conversion improved from 72.1% to 78.9%
• Digital Content subsidiary (Sub 3) has been consistently loss-making with EBITDA of SAR -9M in FY2023, while holding company overhead of SAR -91M (including SAR -85M EBITDA plus eliminations) represents a significant drag on group profitability
• Revenue diversification is strong across six subsidiaries spanning heritage tourism (24.8%), live entertainment (22.9%), cultural real estate (16.7%), arts education (15.2%), creative services (11.9%), and digital content (8.6%) — no single subsidiary exceeds 25% of group revenue
• Critical data gaps exist for ROIC, WACC, interest coverage ratio, debt maturity schedule, working capital components (DSO/DPO), inter-company transfer pricing policies, and detailed capital allocation framework — limiting the depth of financial health assessment

elements.name: Revenue Trajectory
elements.aiAnswer:
• CAG achieved a 5-year revenue CAGR of 32.6% (SAR 680M in FY2019 to SAR 2.1B in FY2023), with FY2022-FY2023 YoY growth of 27.3% — an exceptional growth trajectory driven by both acquisitions and organic expansion
• Revenue is well-diversified across six subsidiaries: Heritage Destinations (SAR 520M, 24.8%), Live Entertainment (SAR 480M, 22.9%), Cultural Real Estate (SAR 350M, 16.7%), Arts Education (SAR 320M, 15.2%), Creative Services (SAR 250M, 11.9%), and Digital Content (SAR 180M, 8.6%) — no single subsidiary exceeds 25% of total revenue
• Fastest-growing subsidiaries are Cultural Real Estate (52.2% YoY), Digital Content (38.5% YoY), and Live Entertainment (37.1% YoY), while Arts Education shows maturity at only 6.7% YoY growth with 'stable enrollment' noted
• Key growth drivers include government concession revenue and ticketing (Heritage), post-COVID recovery and 3 new venues (Entertainment), Phase 1 completion of Al-Fann District (Real Estate), and subscription/licensing models (Digital)
• Revenue concentration risk by client/market is not disclosed — top 5 client concentration data is absent, and geographic market breakdown is unavailable
elements.evidenceQuote: We achieved consolidated revenue of SAR 2.1 billion in FY2023, up from SAR 680 million in FY2019 — a CAGR of 32.6%.
elements.sourceDocument: CAG CORPORATE STRATEGY DOCUMENT 2024.docx
elements.scoreRationale: Revenue growth of 32.6% CAGR over 5 years is exceptional, significantly above the Saudi entertainment sector CAGR of ~11-12%. Revenue diversification across six subsidiaries with no single entity exceeding 25% is strong. Score is capped at 4 rather than 5 due to absence of client concentration data, geographic diversification metrics, and the fact that much growth was acquisition-driven rather than purely organic.
elements.dataGap: Top 5 client revenue concentration percentage; geographic revenue breakdown; organic vs. acquisition-driven revenue split; FY2024 revenue guidance or budget

elements.name: Profitability Analysis
elements.aiAnswer:
• Gross margin was 40.0% in FY2023, recovering from a dip to 39.1% in FY2022 but still below FY2021's 41.2%, suggesting cost pressures from rapid scaling particularly in Entertainment (direct costs SAR 340M on SAR 480M revenue = 70.8% COGS ratio) and Real Estate (57.1% COGS ratio)
• EBITDA grew strongly from SAR 222M (FY2021) to SAR 426M (FY2023), a 36.5% YoY increase; however, Adjusted EBITDA margin has remained flat at 18.2% for three consecutive years (FY2021: 18.2%, FY2022: 18.1%, FY2023: 18.2%), indicating that profitability is not scaling with revenue
• Net profit margin improved from 10.0% (FY2021) to 12.0% (FY2023), with net profit of SAR 251M representing 43.4% YoY growth — the strongest growth metric
• Subsidiary-level EBITDA margins vary significantly: Education leads at 28.1%, followed by Real Estate (25.1%), Heritage (21.9%), Creative (20.0%), Entertainment (15.0%), and Digital is loss-making at -5.0%
• Holding company EBITDA drag is SAR -85M (growing from SAR -55M in FY2021), representing a 54.5% increase in overhead costs over two years — a significant margin erosion factor
• EBIT margin improved from 14.3% to 15.8%, suggesting operating leverage is beginning to materialize despite rising SG&A costs (SAR 112M marketing + SAR 190M G&A + SAR 78M holding overhead = SAR 380M total)
elements.sourceDocument: CAG_Full_Detailed_Financials.xlsx
elements.scoreRationale: While absolute profitability is growing strongly (EBITDA +36.5% YoY, net profit +43.4% YoY), the flat Adjusted EBITDA margin at 18.2% for three consecutive years indicates that profitability is not scaling with revenue growth. The holding company overhead growing from SAR -55M to SAR -85M and the persistently loss-making Digital subsidiary are margin erosion concerns. Score of 3 reflects adequate but not yet strong profitability performance.
elements.dataGap: Peer benchmarking data for cultural economy holding companies; cost breakdown by fixed vs. variable; holding company overhead allocation methodology; Digital Content subsidiary path-to-profitability timeline

elements.name: Liquidity & Solvency
elements.aiAnswer:
• Current ratio has declined steadily from 1.16x (FY2021) to 1.09x (FY2022) to 1.03x (FY2023), approaching the critical 1.0x threshold — the financials explicitly note this as 'Declining'
• Quick ratio has fallen below 1.0x, declining from 0.93x (FY2021) to 0.87x (FY2022) to 0.81x (FY2023), noted as 'Below 1.0' — indicating the entity cannot cover short-term obligations without liquidating inventory or other current assets
• Net debt has increased from SAR 410M (FY2021) to SAR 565M (FY2022) to SAR 720M (FY2023), a 75.6% increase over two years, driven by aggressive capex spending
• Total liabilities grew from SAR 1,058M to SAR 1,758M (66.2% increase), while total equity grew from SAR 915M to SAR 1,258M (37.5% increase), implying a debt-to-equity ratio increasing from approximately 1.16x to 1.40x
• Interest coverage ratio is not disclosed, which is a critical gap given the rising debt levels
• The combination of declining liquidity ratios, rising leverage, and persistently negative free cash flow creates a concerning solvency trajectory that requires close monitoring over the next 12-24 months
elements.evidenceQuote: Current Ratio: 1.16x, 1.09x, 1.03x — Declining; Quick Ratio: 0.93x, 0.87x, 0.81x — Below 1.0; Net Debt: 410, 565, 720 SAR M
elements.sourceDocument: CAG_Full_Detailed_Financials.xlsx
elements.scoreRationale: The declining current ratio approaching 1.0x, quick ratio persistently below 1.0x, and net debt rising 75.6% over two years represent a weak and deteriorating liquidity position. The debt-to-equity ratio has increased from ~1.16x to ~1.40x. Without disclosed interest coverage ratios or debt maturity schedules, the solvency risk cannot be fully assessed but the trajectory is concerning. Score of 2 reflects a weak position with growing risk.
elements.dataGap: Interest coverage ratio; debt maturity schedule and covenants; credit rating; detailed breakdown of current assets and current liabilities; revolving credit facility availability; debt service coverage ratio

elements.name: Cash Flow Quality
elements.aiAnswer:
• Operating cash flow has grown strongly from SAR 160M (FY2021) to SAR 232M (FY2022) to SAR 336M (FY2023), demonstrating improving cash generation capacity
• Cash conversion ratio (OCF/Net Income) improved from 136.8% (FY2021: 160/117) to 132.6% (FY2022: 232/175) to 133.9% (FY2023: 336/251), indicating that operating cash flow consistently exceeds net income — a positive quality-of-earnings indicator
• However, free cash flow has been persistently negative and worsening: SAR -45M (FY2021), SAR -123M (FY2022), SAR -129M (FY2023), driven by heavy capex of SAR 205M, SAR 355M, and SAR 465M respectively
• Capex intensity (capex/revenue) has increased from 17.6% (FY2021) to 21.5% (FY2022) to 22.1% (FY2023), reflecting the investment-heavy phase of portfolio development including 3 new entertainment venues and Phase 1 of Al-Fann District
• The reported cash conversion metric in the financials shows improvement from 72.1% to 74.4% to 78.9%, though the methodology for this calculation differs from the OCF/Net Income ratio
• Non-cash items include D&A of SAR 95M in FY2023 (up from SAR 55M in FY2021), which is significant but expected given the asset-heavy nature of the portfolio
elements.evidenceQuote: Operating Cash Flow: 160, 232, 336; Capex: -205, -355, -465; Free Cash Flow: -45, -123, -129; Cash Conversion: 72.1%, 74.4%, 78.9%
elements.sourceDocument: CAG_Full_Detailed_Financials.xlsx
elements.scoreRationale: Operating cash flow quality is strong with OCF consistently exceeding net income (133.9% ratio in FY2023) and improving cash conversion. However, persistently negative and worsening free cash flow (SAR -129M in FY2023) driven by heavy capex is a concern. The entity is in an investment phase which partially explains the negative FCF, but three consecutive years of negative FCF requires monitoring. Score of 3 reflects adequate cash generation offset by heavy capital consumption.
elements.dataGap: Breakdown of capex between maintenance and growth capex; expected FCF inflection point timeline; financing cash flow details (debt issuance, repayments, dividends); working capital movement details

elements.name: Capital Allocation Efficiency
elements.aiAnswer:
• ROE has improved significantly from 12.4% (FY2021) to 16.2% (FY2022) to 19.8% (FY2023), demonstrating improving returns on equity — though part of this improvement may be leverage-driven given rising debt levels
• ROA can be estimated at approximately 8.3% (FY2023: 251/3016), improving from 5.9% (FY2021: 117/1973), indicating better asset utilization
• ROIC is not disclosed in the documents, which is a critical gap for assessing whether capital allocation is creating value above the cost of capital
• The strategy document references a 'Financial Ambition & Capital Allocation Framework' as a section heading but the detailed content was not provided in the uploaded excerpt
• The strategy document states the holding company 'must earn its right to exist' and that 'every capital allocation decision must demonstrably add value that subsidiaries could not create alone' — indicating strategic awareness of capital efficiency
• Capital projects include 3 new entertainment venues and Phase 1 of Al-Fann District, but no post-investment review data or IRR tracking is available to assess whether these projects delivered expected returns
• Total assets grew from SAR 1,973M to SAR 3,016M (52.9% increase) while revenue grew 80.3% over the same period, suggesting reasonable asset productivity improvement
elements.sourceDocument: CAG_Full_Detailed_Financials.xlsx
elements.scoreRationale: ROE improvement from 12.4% to 19.8% is positive, and the strategy document articulates a clear capital allocation philosophy. However, the absence of ROIC, WACC comparison, and post-investment review data prevents a full assessment of capital efficiency. The improving ROE may be partially leverage-driven. Score of 3 reflects developing capital allocation practices with good directional improvement but insufficient evidence of systematic value creation measurement.
elements.dataGap: ROIC calculation and trend; WACC estimate; post-investment review results for major capital projects; IRR tracking for acquisitions; detailed capital allocation framework criteria and hurdle rates

• Working capital management cannot be meaningfully assessed without these fundamental metrics

P5.description: How well does the entity execute?

elements.name: Core Competencies
elements.aiAnswer: CAG Holding's core competencies are anchored in three material domains: aluminium processing, glass manufacturing, and sustainable packaging. Neuman Aluminium explicitly identifies its core competence as 'the industrial high-quality processing of aluminum' with 'well-trained and skilled employees in production and other specialized fields' forming the core of production facilities **[<490,019dc4cb-ea41-7d56-aaf0-5424a988b1fd>]**. The group has 9,800 employees across 40+ production sites worldwide **[<435,019dc4cb-c638-797a-9630-42a686cb0492>]**. Stoelzle Glass Group brings 200+ years of glassmaking expertise with 3,000 employees producing 3.2 billion glass containers annually across 6 production sites **[<484,019dc4cb-ea3b-725f-9d9a-58f192eac0e6>]**. PREFA contributes 80+ years of aluminium roof and facade system expertise with over 5,000 products **[<441,019dc4cb-b780-76d2-bd3b-71f1d3077765>]**. Neuman Aluminium demonstrates high-value automotive competencies including ADAS sensor housings, radar and camera housings, and lidar components **[<462,019dc4cb-b976-7c6b-8b97-13018e25dc10>]**, with ISO/TS 16949 automotive standards implementation delivering 'high process quality through proven standards, strict project control, preventative error management, and a reliable supply chain' **[<461,019dc4cb-b975-706d-8ecc-bc84c2e4a97b>]**. The holding structure under Dr. Cornelius Alexander Grupp creates synergies: 'Within the CAG-Holding all affiliated companies offer bespoke solutions and all-round competence in processing a whole series of modern materials' **[<484,019dc4cb-ea3b-725f-9d9a-58f192eac0e6>]**. TUBEX adds packaging specialization with 700 million aerosol cans and 1.6 billion aluminium tubes capacity across 7 production sites **[<471,019dc4cb-e9e3-7ca6-a5f1-0f52392da5a0>]**.
elements.evidenceQuote: Our core competence lies in the industrial high-quality processing of aluminum. Thus, well-trained and skilled employees in production and other specialized fields definitely form the core of our production facilities. **[<490,019dc4cb-ea41-7d56-aaf0-5424a988b1fd>]**
elements.scoreRationale: CAG Holding demonstrates clearly identified and leveraged core competencies across its subsidiaries. The group possesses deep expertise in aluminium processing and glass manufacturing with over 200 years of glass heritage (Stoelzle) and 80+ years in aluminium roofing (PREFA). Neuman Aluminium states 'Our core competence lies in the industrial high-quality processing of aluminum' **[<490,019dc4cb-ea41-7d56-aaf0-5424a988b1fd>]**. The competencies are rare (specialized metallurgical knowledge), valuable (serving premium automotive, construction, and packaging markets), and difficult to imitate (decades of accumulated know-how across 40+ production sites). The VRIN criteria are substantially met, though substitutability risk exists from alternative materials like plastics.
elements.dataGap: No formal VRIN analysis or core competency mapping document available at the holding level; competency assessment is inferred from subsidiary-level descriptions rather than a consolidated holding strategy document.

elements.name: Operational Efficiency
elements.aiAnswer: Operational efficiency evidence is primarily available at subsidiary level. Stoelzle Glass Group has implemented a group-wide Process and Energy Data Management System that 'has already led to significant energy savings between 3 percent and 5 percent, by improving the energy efficiency at the sites' **[<452,019dc4cb-bfd7-7d67-bee8-4f60fcc6ac66>]**. Additionally, Stoelzle installed a batch preheater at its Austrian production site that 'reduces furnace energy consumption by over 8 percent and resulting in annual energy savings of 4,000 MWh. The remaining waste heat is fed into the local district heating network, providing heat to approximately 1,800 households' **[<452,019dc4cb-bfd7-7d67-bee8-4f60fcc6ac66>]**. PREFA demonstrates resource efficiency by using '77% Sekundäraluminium' (secondary/recycled aluminium) and since 2020 '100% aus erneuerbarer Energie' (100% renewable energy in production) **[<486,019dc4cb-ea3d-7be5-963a-1a67ec6b7403>]**. Neuman Aluminium implements automotive-grade quality standards: 'consistent implementation of automotive standards in accordance with ISO/TS 16949; this results in high process quality delivered through proven standards, strict project control at new production or technological changes, preventative error management' **[<461,019dc4cb-b975-706d-8ecc-bc84c2e4a97b>]**. The CAG Holding group revenue is reported at EUR 1.56 billion in the Austrian trend TOP500 ranking **[<433,019dc4cb-c636-7d31-b317-78a26b2d2656>]**, with approximately 9,800 employees across 40 facilities **[<435,019dc4cb-c638-797a-9630-42a686cb0492>]**. Stoelzle has received EcoVadis Gold Medal three consecutive times, placing it 'among the top 2% of companies in the glass manufacturing industry (top 5% of all companies)' **[<456,019dc4cb-bfdb-7156-a1ec-0e9dde5cc2b0>]**. No consolidated cost structure, cost-to-revenue ratios, or lean manufacturing program documentation was identified at the holding level.
elements.evidenceQuote: The implementation of the Process and Energy Data Management System at all Stoelzle sites has already led to significant energy savings between 3 percent and 5 percent, by improving the energy efficiency at the sites. **[<452,019dc4cb-bfd7-7d67-bee8-4f60fcc6ac66>]**
elements.scoreRationale: Evidence of operational efficiency exists at subsidiary level but consolidated holding-level metrics are unavailable. Stoelzle's Process and Energy Data Management System achieved 3-5% energy savings **[<452,019dc4cb-bfd7-7d67-bee8-4f60fcc6ac66>]**, and batch preheater technology reduced furnace energy consumption by over 8% (4,000 MWh annual savings) **[<452,019dc4cb-bfd7-7d67-bee8-4f60fcc6ac66>]**. PREFA uses 77% secondary (recycled) aluminium and 100% renewable electricity since 2020 **[<486,019dc4cb-ea3d-7be5-963a-1a67ec6b7403>]**. However, no cost-to-revenue ratios, productivity per employee metrics, or lean/continuous improvement program documentation was found at the holding level. The group's revenue of EUR 1.56 billion **[<433,019dc4cb-c636-7d31-b317-78a26b2d2656>]** across approximately 9,800 employees suggests revenue per employee of approximately EUR 159,000, which is reasonable for industrial manufacturing but cannot be benchmarked without more detail. Score reflects solid subsidiary-level efficiency evidence but significant gaps in consolidated holding metrics.
elements.dataGap: No consolidated holding-level cost-to-revenue ratios, productivity metrics per employee, or lean/continuous improvement program documentation available. Revenue per employee and operating margin data are not publicly disclosed.
