• No compliance gap assessment, regulatory change tracker, PDPL readiness plan, anti-corruption program, whistleblower policy, or compliance training program is documented in available materials
elements.evidenceQuote: Evolving IP frameworks in MENA; entertainment licensing reforms in KSA; data privacy regulations (PDPL) — Compliance investment required; IP protection critical for content subsidiaries
elements.sourceDocument: Cultural Assets Group — Corporate Strategy Plan 2024–2028
elements.scoreRationale: A Legal & Compliance function exists with 10 FTE and an Internal Audit team of 10 FTE reporting to the Audit & Risk Committee **[<81,019dc6f9-fa1c-7daf-8cfe-d7017a68acd3>, <82,019dc6f9-fa1d-79b4-8b9e-eac5dc256ce4>]**. Regulatory risks are identified in the PESTEL analysis **[<27,019dc6f9-f9e6-7777-a7ac-f9d20201dcfe>, <243,019dc6f9-faad-7479-a0ed-260de606b3f9>]**. However, no compliance gap assessment, PDPL readiness plan, regulatory horizon tracker, anti-corruption program, or compliance training documentation exists. The 3-person Compliance & Governance team appears thin for a multi-subsidiary, multi-jurisdiction group.
elements.dataGap: PDPL compliance readiness assessment, regulatory change management tracker, anti-corruption and anti-bribery program documentation, whistleblower policy, compliance training records, and regulatory licenses inventory across all subsidiaries

elements.name: ESG & Sustainability
elements.aiAnswer:
• ESG is mentioned only in the PESTEL environmental scan: 'ESG expectations rising; cultural tourism carbon footprint under scrutiny; green building standards for cultural venues' with the implication 'Must integrate sustainability into operations; potential competitive differentiator' **[<27,019dc6f9-f9e6-7777-a7ac-f9d20201dcfe>, <243,019dc6f9-faad-7479-a0ed-260de606b3f9>, <337,019dc6f9-f79e-704a-a3b9-d7a1d7dd32c7>]**
• The Stewardship core value states 'We are custodians, not owners, of cultural assets — we hold them in trust for future generations' with a behavioral anchor of 'Long-term value creation over extraction' — this provides a philosophical foundation but no operational ESG framework **[<23,019dc6f9-f9e2-79a5-9105-d8cb0984d875>, <266,019dc6f9-fac4-7135-bc0e-8c26118ca0e3>, <458,019dc6fa-00e0-7472-aa30-ee5f0920c439>]**
• Social metrics are partially tracked: Saudization rate 72% (target 80%), gender diversity 34% female group-wide, 43% at GEC level, 22% at Board level **[<70,019dc6f9-fa11-701c-a7a2-a0fd290b6d92>, <95,019dc6f9-fa2a-7bb9-a721-8a680a0509fa>]**
• No ESG strategy, sustainability report, carbon footprint measurement, climate risk assessment, ESG KPIs, ESG reporting framework (GRI/SASB/TCFD), or environmental management system is documented
• Sub 6 (Cultural Real Estate) with 3 major cultural district developments in pipeline has no documented green building commitments or environmental impact assessments
elements.evidenceQuote: ESG expectations rising; cultural tourism carbon footprint under scrutiny; green building standards for cultural venues — Must integrate sustainability into operations; potential competitive differentiator
elements.sourceDocument: Cultural Assets Group — Corporate Strategy Plan 2024–2028
elements.scoreRationale: ESG is acknowledged only as an external environmental factor in the PESTEL analysis **[<27,019dc6f9-f9e6-7777-a7ac-f9d20201dcfe>, <243,019dc6f9-faad-7479-a0ed-260de606b3f9>]** with no dedicated ESG strategy, sustainability report, carbon measurement, climate risk assessment, or ESG reporting framework documented. While some social metrics exist (Saudization, gender diversity) **[<70,019dc6f9-fa11-701c-a7a2-a0fd290b6d92>, <95,019dc6f9-fa2a-7bb9-a721-8a680a0509fa>]**, these are tracked for operational/regulatory reasons rather than as part of a structured ESG program. elements.dataGap: ESG strategy document, sustainability/ESG report, carbon footprint baseline, climate risk assessment (TCFD), ESG KPIs and targets, green building standards for Sub 6 developments, and ESG reporting framework selection

strengths: Board-level Audit & Risk Committee chaired by independent director Dr. Al-Otaibi provides governance oversight of risk **[<52,019dc6f9-f9ff-795e-aa5a-62373ba8e507>, <53,019dc6f9-fa00-7e9f-80e6-bd7c2403df6d>]**

Strategic risks are identified with likelihood/impact ratings and high-level mitigations in the Board-approved strategy document **[<120,019dc6f9-f96c-73e3-a34c-a8df5d098ae0>, <121,019dc6f9-f96d-7296-b8bb-30657bcd9cc0>, <234,019dc6f9-faa4-7355-a840-238ff5eb9301>, <235,019dc6f9-faa5-7384-a0b9-52f48494cce4>]**

Internal Audit function (10 FTE) reports directly to the Audit & Risk Committee with coverage across financial, operational, and IT audit **[<81,019dc6f9-fa1c-7daf-8cfe-d7017a68acd3>, <82,019dc6f9-fa1d-79b4-8b9e-eac5dc256ce4>]**

Experienced Group CLO (Faisal Al-Dosari, Baker McKenzie 12 yrs, SABIC General Counsel 5 yrs) leads the legal and compliance function **[<163,019dc6f9-f997-71ab-bf16-21c64c231f44>, <168,019dc6f9-f99c-7430-88c4-e10dc86e07ea>]**
weaknesses: No dedicated Chief Risk Officer or Group Risk Management function exists in the holding company organizational structure — risk is embedded in strategy rather than managed as a standalone discipline **[<81,019dc6f9-fa1c-7daf-8cfe-d7017a68acd3>, <82,019dc6f9-fa1d-79b4-8b9e-eac5dc256ce4>]**

No Business Continuity Plan, Disaster Recovery Plan, or crisis management framework is documented despite operating physical venues, heritage sites, and digital platforms **[<81,019dc6f9-fa1c-7daf-8cfe-d7017a68acd3>]**

Cybersecurity team of only 5 FTE is under-resourced for a SAR 2.1B group investing SAR 400M in digital transformation across 6 subsidiaries **[<81,019dc6f9-fa1c-7daf-8cfe-d7017a68acd3>, <18,019dc6f9-f9dd-7e30-b052-bb09bdbf787d>]**

ESG is entirely absent as a structured program — no sustainability report, carbon measurement, or ESG KPIs exist **[<27,019dc6f9-f9e6-7777-a7ac-f9d20201dcfe>, <243,019dc6f9-faad-7479-a0ed-260de606b3f9>]**

Matrix reporting between subsidiaries and holding company is inconsistently enforced, creating operational control blind spots **[<70,019dc6f9-fa11-701c-a7a2-a0fd290b6d92>, <95,019dc6f9-fa2a-7bb9-a721-8a680a0509fa>]**
opportunities: Potential IPO of Sub 1 or Sub 6 (2026-2027) creates a forcing function to formalize ERM, compliance, and ESG frameworks to meet listing requirements **[<429,019dc6fa-00c3-7581-be04-0ff6942ae42c>, <225,019dc6f9-fa9b-7a20-b46e-fb916a000c6e>]**

SAR 120M Enterprise Digital Platform initiative (B1) includes cybersecurity upgrade — opportunity to embed comprehensive cyber risk management **[<40,019dc6f9-f9f3-7940-9ff6-b804731c3abb>, <41,019dc6f9-f9f4-79f0-832f-14b98d990f7b>, <109,019dc6f9-f961-712b-82b3-73e9aab17334>, <110,019dc6f9-f962-7ba0-b38b-052706e58229>]**

ESG integration could become a competitive differentiator in the MENA cultural economy as the PESTEL analysis itself notes **[<27,019dc6f9-f9e6-7777-a7ac-f9d20201dcfe>, <243,019dc6f9-faad-7479-a0ed-260de606b3f9>]**
threats: Government policy shift reducing cultural investment rated as Low likelihood but Critical impact — and CAG has significant government revenue dependency **[<120,019dc6f9-f96c-73e3-a34c-a8df5d098ae0>, <121,019dc6f9-f96d-7296-b8bb-30657bcd9cc0>]**

PDPL (Saudi data privacy regulation) compliance requirements with no documented readiness plan, while CAG is building a unified customer data platform (A4, SAR 60M) **[<27,019dc6f9-f9e6-7777-a7ac-f9d20201dcfe>, <243,019dc6f9-faad-7479-a0ed-260de606b3f9>, <39,019dc6f9-f9f2-7a96-b4ed-97033e689064>]**

Geographic expansion into Egypt, Morocco, and Turkey (SAR 340M) introduces multi-jurisdictional regulatory, political, and currency risks with no documented country-risk assessments **[<111,019dc6f9-f963-71ef-914a-5f03b86e4525>, <112,019dc6f9-f964-7fd8-9718-8a7626592019>, <122,019dc6f9-f96e-78dd-ac9d-fee24fac0deb>]**

Talent war for creative/tech professionals in a tight MENA market with Sub 3 (Digital Content) at only 55% Saudization **[<70,019dc6f9-fa11-701c-a7a2-a0fd290b6d92>, <95,019dc6f9-fa2a-7bb9-a721-8a680a0509fa>, <6,019dc6f9-f9d1-79dd-b3c1-f2bfa2accc63>]**

leadership: [Strategic Risks] — The Corporate Strategy Plan documents only 3 strategic risks (R1-R3) **[<120,019dc6f9-f96c-73e3-a34c-a8df5d098ae0>, <121,019dc6f9-f96d-7296-b8bb-30657bcd9cc0>]** — does CAG maintain a more comprehensive enterprise risk register beyond this strategy document, and if so, how many risks are tracked, who owns them, and what is the review cadence?

[Strategic Risks] — Risk R1 (Government policy shift) is rated Low likelihood but Critical impact **[<120,019dc6f9-f96c-73e3-a34c-a8df5d098ae0>, <121,019dc6f9-f96d-7296-b8bb-30657bcd9cc0>]** — given that Saudi Vision 2030 is allocating SAR 50B+ to culture **[<27,019dc6f9-f9e6-7777-a7ac-f9d20201dcfe>]**, what specific early warning indicators does the Board monitor to detect shifts in government cultural investment priorities?

[Operational Risks] — No Business Continuity Plan or Disaster Recovery Plan was found in any available documents — for a group operating physical heritage sites, live entertainment venues, and digital platforms serving millions of visitors, what is the current BCP/DRP status across the group and each subsidiary?

[Operational Risks] — The Group Cybersecurity team has only 5 FTE **[<81,019dc6f9-fa1c-7daf-8cfe-d7017a68acd3>]** while the group is investing SAR 400M in digital transformation **[<18,019dc6f9-f9dd-7e30-b052-bb09bdbf787d>]** and building a unified customer data platform (A4, SAR 60M) **[<39,019dc6f9-f9f2-7a96-b4ed-97033e689064>]** — has a cybersecurity maturity assessment been conducted, and what is the current maturity level?

[Financial Risks] — Net Debt/EBITDA is currently 2.8x against a policy ceiling of 2.5x **[<426,019dc6fa-00c0-7f0c-b8c3-d676fb50cca4>, <429,019dc6fa-00c3-7581-be04-0ff6942ae42c>]** — this means the group is already above its own stated threshold. What is the timeline and plan to bring leverage within the stated policy limit?

[Financial Risks] — Geographic expansion into Egypt, Morocco, and Turkey commits SAR 340M **[<111,019dc6f9-f963-71ef-914a-5f03b86e4525>, <112,019dc6f9-f964-7fd8-9718-8a7626592019>, <122,019dc6f9-f96e-78dd-ac9d-fee24fac0deb>]** across three new currency zones — what FX risk management strategy and hedging instruments are in place or planned, given the Group Treasury has only 4 FTE **[<81,019dc6f9-fa1c-7daf-8cfe-d7017a68acd3>]**?

[Regulatory & Compliance] — The PESTEL analysis identifies PDPL (Saudi data privacy regulation) as a key legal risk **[<27,019dc6f9-f9e6-7777-a7ac-f9d20201dcfe>, <243,019dc6f9-faad-7479-a0ed-260de606b3f9>]**, and initiative A4 is building a unified customer data platform **[<39,019dc6f9-f9f2-7a96-b4ed-97033e689064>]** — what is the current PDPL compliance readiness status, and has a Data Protection Officer been appointed?

[Regulatory & Compliance] — With expansion into 3 new MENA jurisdictions (Egypt, Morocco, Turkey) **[<111,019dc6f9-f963-71ef-914a-5f03b86e4525>, <112,019dc6f9-f964-7fd8-9718-8a7626592019>, <122,019dc6f9-f96e-78dd-ac9d-fee24fac0deb>]**, what regulatory mapping and compliance readiness work has been completed for each target market?

[ESG & Sustainability] — ESG is identified in the PESTEL as a rising expectation **[<27,019dc6f9-f9e6-7777-a7ac-f9d20201dcfe>, <243,019dc6f9-faad-7479-a0ed-260de606b3f9>]** and a potential IPO of Sub 1 or Sub 6 is under evaluation for 2026-2027 **[<429,019dc6fa-00c3-7581-be04-0ff6942ae42c>]** — what is the Board's timeline for developing a formal ESG strategy and sustainability reporting framework to meet potential listing requirements?

[ESG & Sustainability] — Sub 6 (Cultural Real Estate) has a pipeline of 3 major cultural district developments **[<33,019dc6f9-f9ec-7460-b511-692fa519bd33>, <216,019dc6f9-fa92-7a5c-9dbc-bd594dcafbb7>]** — what green building standards or environmental impact assessment requirements have been established for these mega-projects?

[Operational Risks] — The organizational observations note that the matrix reporting between subsidiaries and holding company is 'inconsistently enforced' with 'some subsidiary Finance Directors having minimal interaction with the Group CFO' **[<70,019dc6f9-fa11-701c-a7a2-a0fd290b6d92>, <95,019dc6f9-fa2a-7bb9-a721-8a680a0509fa>]** — what specific actions are being taken to close this governance gap, and how does this affect risk visibility at the holding level?

[Strategic Risks] — Sub 3 (Digital Content) is operating at -5% EBIT margin **[<218,019dc6f9-fa94-7c87-9fe4-ea9fdd2ca588>]** and classified as a Question Mark **[<216,019dc6f9-fa92-7a5c-9dbc-bd594dcafbb7>]** — what are the specific milestone gates that would trigger a strategic exit or write-down decision if the path to profitability by 2026 is not achieved?
team: [Operational Risks] — The Group Cybersecurity team of 5 FTE **[<81,019dc6f9-fa1c-7daf-8cfe-d7017a68acd3>]** is responsible for security across 6 subsidiaries and 2,770 employees — in practice, how are cybersecurity incidents detected, escalated, and resolved across subsidiaries, and has there been a significant incident in the past 12 months?

[Operational Risks] — With no documented BCP/DRP, how do subsidiary operations teams currently handle disruptions to heritage sites (e.g., extreme weather, security incidents) or live entertainment venues (e.g., crowd safety, technical failures)?

[Financial Risks] — The Group Treasury team of 4 FTE **[<81,019dc6f9-fa1c-7daf-8cfe-d7017a68acd3>]** manages financial risk across a SAR 2.1B group — what treasury management systems and controls are currently in place, and how are cash positions across 6 subsidiaries monitored and consolidated?

[Regulatory & Compliance] — The Compliance & Governance team has only 3 FTE **[<81,019dc6f9-fa1c-7daf-8cfe-d7017a68acd3>]** — how are compliance requirements tracked and communicated across 6 subsidiaries operating in different regulatory environments (heritage, entertainment, education, real estate, digital content)?

[Regulatory & Compliance] — Initiative E4 targets exceeding Nitaqat requirements with SAR 25M investment **[<125,019dc6f9-f971-7bf9-a387-e6dc2aca431e>, <126,019dc6f9-f972-717e-aa61-1192fb681968>]** — what is the current Saudization compliance status by subsidiary, and which subsidiaries are at risk of falling below minimum thresholds?

[ESG & Sustainability] — Heritage Destinations Co. (Sub 1) manages heritage sites with 850 FTE **[<60,019dc6f9-fa07-7597-8c9b-929f57382cf3>]** — what environmental management practices (waste, energy, water) are currently in place at heritage sites, and are any metrics being tracked?

[Operational Risks] — The organizational structure notes the Group CEO has 12 direct reports at the 'upper limit of effective span' **[<70,019dc6f9-fa11-701c-a7a2-a0fd290b6d92>, <95,019dc6f9-fa2a-7bb9-a721-8a680a0509fa>]** — in practice, how does this affect the speed and quality of risk-related decision-making at the holding level?

[Strategic Risks] — The strategy document notes 'talent war for creative/tech professionals' as a threat **[<6,019dc6f9-f9d1-79dd-b3c1-f2bfa2accc63>]** and Sub 3 (Digital Content) has only 55% Saudization **[<70,019dc6f9-fa11-701c-a7a2-a0fd290b6d92>]** — what is the current voluntary turnover rate for tech roles across the group, and what retention measures beyond the Leadership Academy are operational?

[Financial Risks] — Sub 2 (Live Entertainment) has a 15% EBIT margin **[<218,019dc6f9-fa94-7c87-9fe4-ea9fdd2ca588>]** while pursuing aggressive venue expansion — how are project cost overruns and revenue shortfalls monitored and escalated for the venue expansion program?

[Regulatory & Compliance] — The Internal Audit team of 10 FTE **[<81,019dc6f9-fa1c-7daf-8cfe-d7017a68acd3>]** covers financial, operational, and IT audit — what was the most recent audit cycle's key findings, and how are audit recommendations tracked to closure?

gapFilling.question: Does the Group Treasury function maintain a formal Treasury Risk Management Policy covering FX risk, interest rate risk, counterparty credit limits, and liquidity management? If so, please provide the policy document and most recent liquidity stress test results.

gapFilling.question: Has CAG developed any ESG-related documentation including an ESG strategy, sustainability report, carbon footprint baseline measurement, or ESG materiality assessment? If any exist in draft form, please provide them.

P8.name: Growth & Strategic Options
P8.description: Where are the opportunities for value creation?

execSummary.aiDraft:
• CAG has a comprehensive, board-approved growth strategy (2024-2028) targeting SAR 3,600M revenue from SAR 2,100M (71% growth), with five clearly defined strategic pillars covering synergy acceleration, digital transformation, geographic expansion, operational excellence, and talent **[<5,019dc6f9-f8f1-761f-9192-be4a12519bee>, <29,019dc6f9-f909-71e3-8c2b-443ed611e7fd>, <50,019dc6f9-f91e-7999-9dd7-99566738d2ec>]**
• Organic growth vectors are well-articulated across all four Ansoff quadrants: market penetration via Cultural Passport 2.0 (SAR 35M investment, SAR 80M expected by 2027), market development into Egypt/Morocco/Turkey (SAR 340M allocated), product development via AI-native content and digital twins, and related diversification governed by the Cultural Nexus Test **[<12,019dc6f9-f8f8-7905-bc1c-fc3f536a4d59>, <36,019dc6f9-f910-7a49-8c08-351bd3558575>, <34,019dc6f9-f90e-7077-93e5-9b884449fa9e>, <17,019dc6f9-f8fd-71e5-ad9a-3c91865b2811>]**
• Inorganic growth strategy is underdeveloped — the first cycle (2019-2023) involved acquiring 4 subsidiaries and incubating 2, but the 2024-2028 plan contains no explicit M&A pipeline, acquisition criteria, or target list; only SAR 60M (3%) allocated to Innovation & Ventures **[<5,019dc6f9-f8f1-761f-9192-be4a12519bee>, <52,019dc6f9-f920-7c07-b5fb-d725c039331e>]**
• Digital & AI strategy is exceptionally detailed with SAR 360M allocated (18% of capital envelope) across four initiatives: Enterprise Digital Platform (SAR 120M), AI-Powered Cultural Experiences (SAR 80M), Digital Twin Cultural Assets (SAR 55M), and Operational AI (SAR 45M) **[<34,019dc6f9-f90e-7077-93e5-9b884449fa9e>, <35,019dc6f9-f90f-7c25-a56a-a43143371d46>, <51,019dc6f9-f91f-79ab-b077-9e73a08fd931>]**
• Portfolio optimization is strong with BCG-inspired classification (3 Stars, 1 Question Mark, 2 Cash Cows), clear capital allocation logic, and potential IPO of Sub 1 or Sub 6 under evaluation for 2026-2027 **[<27,019dc6f9-f907-7685-b94f-1e7b56731438>, <53,019dc6f9-f921-7ea1-84bc-1957c369ae2d>]**; however, parenting advantage framework, while articulated with 5 value creation mechanisms, acknowledges synergies are underexploited (SAR 28M in FY2023 vs. SAR 200M target) and holding overhead is questioned by some board members **[<9,019dc6f9-f8f5-76f1-a529-01612bfe250c>, <14,019dc6f9-f8fa-7243-a85a-91237f5ab2b1>]**

elements.name: Organic Growth Vectors
elements.aiAnswer:
• Market Penetration: Cultural Passport 2.0 unified ticketing & membership across all subsidiaries (SAR 35M investment, SAR 80M annual revenue by 2027) **[<12,019dc6f9-f8f8-7905-bc1c-fc3f536a4d59>, <13,019dc6f9-f8f9-7a69-b16e-e85394b94e3a>]**; Cross-subsidiary corporate sales team targeting SAR 55M in B2B revenue (SAR 8M investment) **[<33,019dc6f9-f90d-7531-b1a0-048cd8cb6607>]**; Shared Content Studio (SAR 50M investment) **[<33,019dc6f9-f90d-7531-b1a0-048cd8cb6607>]**
• Market Development: Strategic Pillar C targets 3 new MENA markets by 2028 contributing 15% of group revenue — Egypt (SAR 200M, heritage tourism & cultural real estate), Morocco (SAR 80M, live entertainment & arts education), Turkey (SAR 60M, digital content & creative services) **[<36,019dc6f9-f910-7a49-8c08-351bd3558575>, <37,019dc6f9-f911-7dc8-a4e7-d99158d6ac48>, <44,019dc6f9-f918-7d3f-8531-626afa335814>]**
• Product Development: AI-Powered Cultural Experiences via generative AI for personalized tours, content, education (SAR 80M) **[<34,019dc6f9-f90e-7077-93e5-9b884449fa9e>, <35,019dc6f9-f90f-7c25-a56a-a43143371d46>]**; Digital Twin Cultural Assets via VR/AR replicas (SAR 55M) **[<35,019dc6f9-f90f-7c25-a56a-a43143371d46>]**; Sub 3 mandated to pivot to AI-native content **[<27,019dc6f9-f907-7685-b94f-1e7b56731438>]**
• Diversification: Explicitly governed by the Cultural Nexus Test — any future acquisition or incubation must pass the test: 'Does this entity's core business fundamentally depend on, or contribute to, the cultural economy?' **[<17,019dc6f9-f8fd-71e5-ad9a-3c91865b2811>]**; Related-Linked Diversification strategy confirmed **[<15,019dc6f9-f8fb-7d70-93c2-f439170d2be6>]**
• Revenue growth target: SAR 2,100M to SAR 3,600M (CAGR ~11.4%) with EBITDA margin improvement from 18.2% to 24.0% **[<29,019dc6f9-f909-71e3-8c2b-443ed611e7fd>, <50,019dc6f9-f91e-7999-9dd7-99566738d2ec>]**

Document Title: Cultural Assets Group — Corporate Strategy Plan 2024–2028 Classification: Confidential — Board Approved Version: 3.2 Final Date: January 15, 2024 Prepared by: Office of the Group CEO & Group Strategy DivisionApproved by: CAG Board of Directors — Resolution #BD-2024-003 (January 12, 2024) Format: PDF (48 pages)



TABLE OF CONTENTS

Chairman's Foreword

Group CEO's Strategic Letter

Who We Are — Mission, Vision & Values

Our Theory of Value Creation (Parenting Purpose)

Strategic Context & Environmental Scan

Group Strategic Pillars 2024–2028

Portfolio Strategy & Subsidiary Mandates

Financial Ambition & Capital Allocation Framework

Governance of Strategy Execution

Key Risks to Strategy

Appendices



1. CHAIRMAN'S FOREWORD

The Cultural Assets Group stands at an inflection point. Over the past decade, we have assembled a portfolio of six distinctive subsidiaries operating across the cultural economy — spanning heritage tourism, live entertainment, digital content, arts education, cultural real estate development, and creative services. Each subsidiary was acquired or incubated because of its intrinsic connection to culture as an asset class.

As I reflect on our journey, I am proud of what we have built but clear-eyed about what lies ahead. The global cultural economy is projected to reach USD 8.2 trillion by 2028 (UNESCO/Oxford Economics, 2023). Yet this growth will not be evenly distributed. It will accrue to organizations that can operate at the intersection of authenticity, technology, and scale — precisely where CAG is positioned.

This strategy document represents the Board's consensus on where we are headed and how we will get there. It is the product of six months of deliberation, subsidiary consultations, external advisory input, and rigorous financial modeling.

Sheikh Ahmed Al-Farsi Chairman, CAG Board of Directors



2. GROUP CEO'S STRATEGIC LETTER

To our Board, leadership teams, and stakeholders:

Our first strategic cycle (2019–2023) was defined by portfolio assembly. We acquired four subsidiaries, incubated two, and established the holding company's central functions. We achieved consolidated revenue of SAR 2.1 billion in FY2023, up from SAR 680 million in FY2019 — a CAGR of 32.6%.

Our second strategic cycle (2024–2028) must be defined by portfolio optimization and value multiplication. We must shift from "collection" to "connection" — unlocking the synergies between our subsidiaries that justified their acquisition in the first place.

Three convictions underpin this strategy:

Culture is the new infrastructure. Governments and consumers are investing in cultural experiences at unprecedented rates. Our subsidiaries sit on irreplaceable cultural assets.

The holding company must earn its right to exist. Every central function, every governance mechanism, every capital allocation decision must demonstrably add value that subsidiaries could not create alone.

Digital is not a pillar — it is the atmosphere. Every subsidiary strategy must be digitally native. We will invest SAR 400 million over five years in digital transformation across the group.

Nora Al-Rashid Group CEO, Cultural Assets Group



3. WHO WE ARE — MISSION, VISION & VALUES

3.1 Mission Statement

"To preserve, activate, and scale cultural assets for the enrichment of communities and the creation of sustainable economic value."

3.2 Vision Statement

"By 2028, CAG will be the Middle East and North Africa's leading cultural economy group — recognized for the authenticity of our cultural offerings, the excellence of our operations, and the impact of our investments on communities and stakeholders."

3.3 Core Values

Value

Definition

Behavioral Anchor

Authenticity

We honor the integrity of cultural assets and never compromise heritage for short-term gain

Every product/experience must pass the "Cultural Integrity Review"

Excellence

We pursue operational and creative excellence in everything we do

Zero tolerance for mediocrity; continuous improvement embedded in KPIs

Stewardship

We are custodians, not owners, of cultural assets — we hold them in trust for future generations

Long-term value creation over short-term extraction

Collaboration

We believe the group is greater than the sum of its parts

Cross-subsidiary projects are rewarded; silos are actively dismantled

Courage

We take bold, calculated bets on the future of culture

Innovation budget ring-fenced; failure-tolerant experimentation encouraged

3.4 Strategic Identity Summary

CAG is a strategic holding company (not a financial holding or passive investor). We actively shape subsidiary strategies, allocate capital with conviction, provide shared services where scale advantages exist, and intervene when subsidiaries underperform. Our parenting style is best described as "Strategic Architect" — we set the blueprint, resource the build, and monitor progress, but we empower subsidiary CEOs to lead execution.



4. OUR THEORY OF VALUE CREATION (PARENTING PURPOSE)

4.1 The Parenting Advantage Framework

CAG creates value for its subsidiaries through five mechanisms:

#

Value Creation Mechanism

Description

Example

1

Capital Allocation

Centralized capital allocation enables investment in highest-return opportunities across the portfolio, rather than each subsidiary self-funding

SAR 120M redirected from Subsidiary 4 (mature, cash-generative) to Subsidiary 2 (high-growth, capital-hungry) in 2023

2

Talent & Leadership Development

Group-wide talent pool, leadership rotation program, and centralized executive recruitment

Group CHRO manages top-50 leadership pipeline; 3 subsidiary CEOs rotated in 2022–2023

3

Shared Services & Scale Economies

Centralized procurement, finance, legal, IT infrastructure, and marketing analytics

Group procurement saved SAR 45M in FY2023 through consolidated vendor contracts

4

Brand & Reputation Halo

The CAG brand provides credibility, government access, and partnership leverage that individual subsidiaries could not achieve alone

CAG brand enabled Subsidiary 1 to secure a 25-year government concession valued at SAR 800M

5

Strategic Synergy Orchestration

Active identification and execution of cross-subsidiary revenue and cost synergies

"Cultural Passport" product (cross-selling across Subsidiaries 1, 2, and 5) generated SAR 28M incremental revenue in FY2023

4.2 Corporate-Level Strategy

CAG's corporate-level strategy is a Related-Linked Diversification strategy. Our subsidiaries are linked by:

A common focus on cultural assets as the core resource

Shared customer segments (cultural tourists, experience seekers, government/institutional buyers)

Complementary capabilities (content creation, venue management, digital distribution, education)

Geographic overlap (primarily MENA, with selective international expansion)

We explicitly reject unrelated diversification. Any future acquisition or incubation must pass the "Cultural Nexus Test": Does this entity's core business fundamentally depend on, or contribute to, the cultural economy?



5. STRATEGIC CONTEXT & ENVIRONMENTAL SCAN

5.1 Macro-Environmental Analysis (PESTEL)

Factor

Key Trends

Implication for CAG

Time Horizon

Political

Saudi Vision 2030 allocating SAR 50B+ to culture & entertainment; UAE cultural investment accelerating; Egypt cultural heritage monetization

Massive tailwind; government as customer, partner, and regulator simultaneously

2024–2030

Economic

MENA GDP growth 3.2% (IMF 2024); tourism recovery post-COVID at 112% of 2019 levels; inflation moderating to 2.8%

Favorable demand environment; cost pressures easing

2024–2026

Social

Youth demographic bulge (65% under 35 in KSA); rising demand for experiential consumption; cultural identity as social currency

Core demand driver; product design must be youth-centric and Instagram-worthy

Structural

Opportunity and threat; must invest or be disrupted

2024–2028

Environmental

ESG expectations rising; cultural tourism carbon footprint under scrutiny; green building standards for cultural venues

Must integrate sustainability into operations; potential competitive differentiator

2024–2028

Legal

Evolving IP frameworks in MENA; entertainment licensing reforms in KSA; data privacy regulations (PDPL)

Compliance investment required; IP protection critical for content subsidiaries

2024–2026

5.2 Industry Analysis — Cultural Economy Value Chain

The cultural economy value chain consists of four layers:

Cultural Asset Origination — Heritage sites, artistic creation, IP development

Cultural Asset Activation — Experiences, events, exhibitions, education

Cultural Asset Distribution — Digital platforms, media, licensing, merchandising

Cultural Asset Monetization — Ticketing, sponsorship, real estate, government contracts

CAG's portfolio spans all four layers, which is a distinctive competitive advantage. Most competitors operate in one or two layers.

CAG's competitive position: #2 in MENA cultural economy by revenue (private sector); #1 in breadth of value chain coverage.

5.4 SWOT Summary (Pre-Assessment — CEO's Perspective)



Positive

Internal

Strengths: Unique portfolio spanning full cultural value chain; strong government relationships; SAR 2.1B revenue base; talented subsidiary CEOs

Weaknesses: Synergies underexploited; digital maturity uneven across subsidiaries; holding company overhead questioned by some board members; financial reporting not yet fully consolidated in real-time

External

Opportunities: Vision 2030 cultural investment wave; digital/AI transformation of cultural experiences; international expansion (Egypt, Morocco, Turkey); "Cultural Passport" product scaling

Threats: Government entities competing directly; talent war for creative/tech professionals; regulatory uncertainty in new markets; economic downturn reducing discretionary cultural spending

Span of Control: Group CEO has 12 direct reports (6 GEC + 6 Subsidiary CEOs) — at the upper limit of effective span. Consider adding a Group Deputy CEO or COO with subsidiary oversight responsibility.

TABLE OF CONTENTS

CEO's Strategic Letter

Who We Are — Mission, Vision & Values

Appendices



1. CEO'S STRATEGIC LETTER

To the Heritage Destinations Subsidiary Board, Group CEO, and our teams:

Heritage Destinations Co. is the crown jewel of the Cultural Assets Group portfolio. We operate five heritage sites across Saudi Arabia under long-term government concessions, including the flagship Al-Madinah Heritage Quarter — a 25-year concession valued at SAR 800M that we secured in 2021 with the support of the CAG brand and government relationships.

In FY2023, we delivered revenue of SAR 520M and Adjusted EBITDA of SAR 114M (21.9% margin). We welcomed 3.8 million visitors across our sites, a 42% increase from FY2022. Our Net Promoter Score reached 67, placing us in the top quartile of global heritage tourism operators.

Yet I am not satisfied. Our EBITDA margin declined from 23.2% in FY2021 to 21.9% in FY2023, even as revenue grew 67.7% over the same period. This margin compression reflects the cost of scaling — new site openings, staffing ramp-ups, and infrastructure investments. The next strategic cycle must reverse this trend.

Our 2024–2028 strategy is built on three pillars:

Deepen the visitor experience — move from "visit" to "immersion" through technology, storytelling, and personalization. Our target: increase average revenue per visitor from SAR 137 to SAR 210 by 2028.

Scale sustainably — expand to 8 heritage sites (adding 3 new concessions) while improving EBITDA margin to 28% through operational excellence and digital efficiency.

Become the global benchmark — position Heritage Destinations as the reference standard for heritage tourism worldwide, attracting international partnerships, UNESCO recognition, and inbound cultural tourism.

This strategy is fully aligned with CAG's Corporate Strategy, particularly Strategic Pillars A (Portfolio Synergy Acceleration), B (Digital Transformation), and C (Geographic Expansion — Egypt market entry is a joint initiative with Sub 6).

Ahmad Al-Harthy CEO, Heritage Destinations Co.



2. WHO WE ARE — MISSION, VISION & VALUES

2.1 Mission Statement

"To bring heritage to life — creating world-class visitor experiences that honor the past, engage the present, and inspire the future."

2.2 Vision Statement

"By 2028, Heritage Destinations will be the Middle East's most admired heritage tourism operator and a globally recognized model for sustainable cultural tourism."

2.3 Core Values

Value

Definition

Behavioral Anchor

Authenticity

We never compromise the integrity of heritage for commercial gain

Every experience passes the Heritage Integrity Review; academic advisory board validates all content

Hospitality

We treat every visitor as an honored guest

Visitor satisfaction KPIs embedded in all staff performance reviews; mystery visitor program

Preservation

We are custodians of irreplaceable cultural assets

Conservation budget ring-fenced at minimum 8% of revenue; annual heritage condition reports

Innovation

We use technology to enhance, not replace, the human connection to heritage

Digital experiences complement physical visits; AR/VR used to reveal hidden stories

Community

We create value for the communities surrounding our heritage sites

Local hiring targets (60%+); community benefit-sharing agreements at each site

2.4 Strategic Identity

Heritage Destinations Co. is a heritage tourism operator and cultural experience company. We hold long-term government concessions to manage, conserve, and commercially activate heritage sites. Our business model combines:

Concession revenue (government payments for site management)

Visitor revenue (ticketing, guided experiences, retail, F&B)

Partnership revenue (corporate events, film location licensing, educational programs)

Digital revenue (virtual tours, digital content licensing, NFT collectibles — emerging)

Document Title: Cultural Assets Group — Corporate Strategy Plan 2024–2028 Classification: Confidential — Board Approved Version: 3.2 Final Date: January 15, 2024 Prepared by: Office of the Group CEO & Group Strategy DivisionApproved by: CAG Board of Directors — Resolution #BD-2024-003 (January 12, 2024) Format: PDF (48 pages)



TABLE OF CONTENTS

Chairman's Foreword

Group CEO's Strategic Letter

Who We Are — Mission, Vision & Values

Our Theory of Value Creation (Parenting Purpose)

Strategic Context & Environmental Scan

Group Strategic Pillars 2024–2028

Portfolio Strategy & Subsidiary Mandates

Financial Ambition & Capital Allocation Framework

Governance of Strategy Execution

Key Risks to Strategy

Appendices



1. CHAIRMAN'S FOREWORD

The Cultural Assets Group stands at an inflection point. Over the past decade, we have assembled a portfolio of six distinctive subsidiaries operating across the cultural economy — spanning heritage tourism, live entertainment, digital content, arts education, cultural real estate development, and creative services. Each subsidiary was acquired or incubated because of its intrinsic connection to culture as an asset class.

As I reflect on our journey, I am proud of what we have built but clear-eyed about what lies ahead. The global cultural economy is projected to reach USD 8.2 trillion by 2028 (UNESCO/Oxford Economics, 2023). Yet this growth will not be evenly distributed. It will accrue to organizations that can operate at the intersection of authenticity, technology, and scale — precisely where CAG is positioned.

This strategy document represents the Board's consensus on where we are headed and how we will get there. It is the product of six months of deliberation, subsidiary consultations, external advisory input, and rigorous financial modeling.

Sheikh Ahmed Al-Farsi Chairman, CAG Board of Directors



2. GROUP CEO'S STRATEGIC LETTER

To our Board, leadership teams, and stakeholders:

Our first strategic cycle (2019–2023) was defined by portfolio assembly. We acquired four subsidiaries, incubated two, and established the holding company's central functions. We achieved consolidated revenue of SAR 2.1 billion in FY2023, up from SAR 680 million in FY2019 — a CAGR of 32.6%.

Our second strategic cycle (2024–2028) must be defined by portfolio optimization and value multiplication. We must shift from "collection" to "connection" — unlocking the synergies between our subsidiaries that justified their acquisition in the first place.

Three convictions underpin this strategy:

Culture is the new infrastructure. Governments and consumers are investing in cultural experiences at unprecedented rates. Our subsidiaries sit on irreplaceable cultural assets.

The holding company must earn its right to exist. Every central function, every governance mechanism, every capital allocation decision must demonstrably add value that subsidiaries could not create alone.

Digital is not a pillar — it is the atmosphere. Every subsidiary strategy must be digitally native. We will invest SAR 400 million over five years in digital transformation across the group.

Nora Al-Rashid Group CEO, Cultural Assets Group



3. WHO WE ARE — MISSION, VISION & VALUES

3.1 Mission Statement

"To preserve, activate, and scale cultural assets for the enrichment of communities and the creation of sustainable economic value."

3.2 Vision Statement

"By 2028, CAG will be the Middle East and North Africa's leading cultural economy group — recognized for the authenticity of our cultural offerings, the excellence of our operations, and the impact of our investments on communities and stakeholders."

3.3 Core Values

Value

Definition

Behavioral Anchor

Authenticity

We honor the integrity of cultural assets and never compromise heritage for short-term gain

Every product/experience must pass the "Cultural Integrity Review"

Excellence

We pursue operational and creative excellence in everything we do

Zero tolerance for mediocrity; continuous improvement embedded in KPIs

Stewardship

We are custodians, not owners, of cultural assets — we hold them in trust for future generations

Long-term value creation over short-term extraction

Collaboration

We believe the group is greater than the sum of its parts

Cross-subsidiary projects are rewarded; silos are actively dismantled

Courage

We take bold, calculated bets on the future of culture

Innovation budget ring-fenced; failure-tolerant experimentation encouraged

3.4 Strategic Identity Summary

CAG is a strategic holding company (not a financial holding or passive investor). We actively shape subsidiary strategies, allocate capital with conviction, provide shared services where scale advantages exist, and intervene when subsidiaries underperform. Our parenting style is best described as "Strategic Architect" — we set the blueprint, resource the build, and monitor progress, but we empower subsidiary CEOs to lead execution.



4. OUR THEORY OF VALUE CREATION (PARENTING PURPOSE)

4.1 The Parenting Advantage Framework

CAG creates value for its subsidiaries through five mechanisms:

#

Value Creation Mechanism

Description

Example

1

Capital Allocation

Centralized capital allocation enables investment in highest-return opportunities across the portfolio, rather than each subsidiary self-funding

SAR 120M redirected from Subsidiary 4 (mature, cash-generative) to Subsidiary 2 (high-growth, capital-hungry) in 2023

2

Talent & Leadership Development

Group-wide talent pool, leadership rotation program, and centralized executive recruitment

Group CHRO manages top-50 leadership pipeline; 3 subsidiary CEOs rotated in 2022–2023

3

Shared Services & Scale Economies

Centralized procurement, finance, legal, IT infrastructure, and marketing analytics

Group procurement saved SAR 45M in FY2023 through consolidated vendor contracts

4

Brand & Reputation Halo

The CAG brand provides credibility, government access, and partnership leverage that individual subsidiaries could not achieve alone

CAG brand enabled Subsidiary 1 to secure a 25-year government concession valued at SAR 800M

5

Strategic Synergy Orchestration

Active identification and execution of cross-subsidiary revenue and cost synergies

"Cultural Passport" product (cross-selling across Subsidiaries 1, 2, and 5) generated SAR 28M incremental revenue in FY2023

4.2 Corporate-Level Strategy

CAG's corporate-level strategy is a Related-Linked Diversification strategy. Our subsidiaries are linked by:

A common focus on cultural assets as the core resource

Shared customer segments (cultural tourists, experience seekers, government/institutional buyers)

Complementary capabilities (content creation, venue management, digital distribution, education)

Geographic overlap (primarily MENA, with selective international expansion)

We explicitly reject unrelated diversification. Any future acquisition or incubation must pass the "Cultural Nexus Test": Does this entity's core business fundamentally depend on, or contribute to, the cultural economy?



5. STRATEGIC CONTEXT & ENVIRONMENTAL SCAN

5.1 Macro-Environmental Analysis (PESTEL)

Massive tailwind; government as customer, partner, and regulator simultaneously

Favorable demand environment; cost pressures easing

Youth demographic bulge (65% under 35 in KSA); rising demand for experiential consumption; cultural identity as social currency

2024–2028

2024–2026

5.2 Industry Analysis — Cultural Economy Value Chain

The cultural economy value chain consists of four layers:

Cultural Asset Origination — Heritage sites, artistic creation, IP development

Cultural Asset Activation — Experiences, events, exhibitions, education

Cultural Asset Distribution — Digital platforms, media, licensing, merchandising

Cultural Asset Monetization — Ticketing, sponsorship, real estate, government contracts

CAG's portfolio spans all four layers, which is a distinctive competitive advantage. Most competitors operate in one or two layers.

KEY ORGANIZATIONAL OBSERVATIONS

Span of Control: Group CEO has 12 direct reports (6 GEC + 6 Subsidiary CEOs) — at the upper limit of effective span. Consider adding a Group Deputy CEO or COO with subsidiary oversight responsibility.

Saudization: Group-wide Saudization rate is 72% (target: 80% by 2026). Highest in Sub 4 (Arts Education, 85%) and lowest in Sub 3 (Digital Content, 55% — tech talent scarcity).

Gender Diversity: 34% female across group; 43% at GEC level (3 of 7); 33% at Subsidiary CEO level (2 of 6). Board: 22% female (2 of 9).

Average Tenure: GEC average tenure is 3.0 years (relatively new team). Subsidiary CEO average tenure is 3.5 years. Longest-serving: Dr. Mona Al-Turki (Sub 4, 5 years). Shortest: Yara Al-Amri (Group CMO, 1 year).

Holding Company Overhead: 120 FTE at SAR 42M cost represents 2.0% of group revenue. Benchmark for strategic holding companies is 1.5–2.5% — CAG is within range but should monitor as revenue scales.

Reporting Matrix: Subsidiary functional heads (Finance, HR) have a solid line to their Subsidiary CEO and a dotted line to the corresponding Group function head. This creates a matrix that enables group standards while preserving subsidiary autonomy. However, interviews suggest the dotted line is inconsistently enforced — some subsidiary Finance Directors have minimal interaction with the Group CFO.

1. CEO'S STRATEGIC LETTER

To the Heritage Destinations Subsidiary Board, Group CEO, and our teams:

Heritage Destinations Co. is the crown jewel of the Cultural Assets Group portfolio. We operate five heritage sites across Saudi Arabia under long-term government concessions, including the flagship Al-Madinah Heritage Quarter — a 25-year concession valued at SAR 800M that we secured in 2021 with the support of the CAG brand and government relationships.

In FY2023, we delivered revenue of SAR 520M and Adjusted EBITDA of SAR 114M (21.9% margin). We welcomed 3.8 million visitors across our sites, a 42% increase from FY2022. Our Net Promoter Score reached 67, placing us in the top quartile of global heritage tourism operators.

Yet I am not satisfied. Our EBITDA margin declined from 23.2% in FY2021 to 21.9% in FY2023, even as revenue grew 67.7% over the same period. This margin compression reflects the cost of scaling — new site openings, staffing ramp-ups, and infrastructure investments. The next strategic cycle must reverse this trend.

Our 2024–2028 strategy is built on three pillars:

Deepen the visitor experience — move from "visit" to "immersion" through technology, storytelling, and personalization. Our target: increase average revenue per visitor from SAR 137 to SAR 210 by 2028.

Scale sustainably — expand to 8 heritage sites (adding 3 new concessions) while improving EBITDA margin to 28% through operational excellence and digital efficiency.

Become the global benchmark — position Heritage Destinations as the reference standard for heritage tourism worldwide, attracting international partnerships, UNESCO recognition, and inbound cultural tourism.

This strategy is fully aligned with CAG's Corporate Strategy, particularly Strategic Pillars A (Portfolio Synergy Acceleration), B (Digital Transformation), and C (Geographic Expansion — Egypt market entry is a joint initiative with Sub 6).

Ahmad Al-Harthy CEO, Heritage Destinations Co.



2. WHO WE ARE — MISSION, VISION & VALUES

2.1 Mission Statement

"To bring heritage to life — creating world-class visitor experiences that honor the past, engage the present, and inspire the future."

2.2 Vision Statement

"By 2028, Heritage Destinations will be the Middle East's most admired heritage tourism operator and a globally recognized model for sustainable cultural tourism."

2.3 Core Values

Value

Definition

Behavioral Anchor

Authenticity

We never compromise the integrity of heritage for commercial gain

Every experience passes the Heritage Integrity Review; academic advisory board validates all content

Hospitality

We treat every visitor as an honored guest

Visitor satisfaction KPIs embedded in all staff performance reviews; mystery visitor program

Preservation

We are custodians of irreplaceable cultural assets

Conservation budget ring-fenced at minimum 8% of revenue; annual heritage condition reports

Innovation

We use technology to enhance, not replace, the human connection to heritage

Digital experiences complement physical visits; AR/VR used to reveal hidden stories

Community

We create value for the communities surrounding our heritage sites

Local hiring targets (60%+); community benefit-sharing agreements at each site

2.4 Strategic Identity

Heritage Destinations Co. is a heritage tourism operator and cultural experience company. We hold long-term government concessions to manage, conserve, and commercially activate heritage sites. Our business model combines:

Concession revenue (government payments for site management)

Visitor revenue (ticketing, guided experiences, retail, F&B)

Partnership revenue (corporate events, film location licensing, educational programs)

Digital revenue (virtual tours, digital content licensing, NFT collectibles — emerging)

Document Title: Cultural Assets Group — Corporate Strategy Plan 2024–2028 Classification: Confidential — Board Approved Version: 3.2 Final Date: January 15, 2024 Prepared by: Office of the Group CEO & Group Strategy DivisionApproved by: CAG Board of Directors — Resolution #BD-2024-003 (January 12, 2024) Format: PDF (48 pages)



TABLE OF CONTENTS

Chairman's Foreword

Group CEO's Strategic Letter

Who We Are — Mission, Vision & Values

Our Theory of Value Creation (Parenting Purpose)

Strategic Context & Environmental Scan

Group Strategic Pillars 2024–2028

Portfolio Strategy & Subsidiary Mandates

Financial Ambition & Capital Allocation Framework

Governance of Strategy Execution

Key Risks to Strategy

Appendices



1. CHAIRMAN'S FOREWORD

The Cultural Assets Group stands at an inflection point. Over the past decade, we have assembled a portfolio of six distinctive subsidiaries operating across the cultural economy — spanning heritage tourism, live entertainment, digital content, arts education, cultural real estate development, and creative services. Each subsidiary was acquired or incubated because of its intrinsic connection to culture as an asset class.

As I reflect on our journey, I am proud of what we have built but clear-eyed about what lies ahead. The global cultural economy is projected to reach USD 8.2 trillion by 2028 (UNESCO/Oxford Economics, 2023). Yet this growth will not be evenly distributed. It will accrue to organizations that can operate at the intersection of authenticity, technology, and scale — precisely where CAG is positioned.

This strategy document represents the Board's consensus on where we are headed and how we will get there. It is the product of six months of deliberation, subsidiary consultations, external advisory input, and rigorous financial modeling.

Sheikh Ahmed Al-Farsi Chairman, CAG Board of Directors



2. GROUP CEO'S STRATEGIC LETTER

To our Board, leadership teams, and stakeholders:

Our first strategic cycle (2019–2023) was defined by portfolio assembly. We acquired four subsidiaries, incubated two, and established the holding company's central functions. We achieved consolidated revenue of SAR 2.1 billion in FY2023, up from SAR 680 million in FY2019 — a CAGR of 32.6%.

Our second strategic cycle (2024–2028) must be defined by portfolio optimization and value multiplication. We must shift from "collection" to "connection" — unlocking the synergies between our subsidiaries that justified their acquisition in the first place.

Three convictions underpin this strategy:

Culture is the new infrastructure. Governments and consumers are investing in cultural experiences at unprecedented rates. Our subsidiaries sit on irreplaceable cultural assets.

The holding company must earn its right to exist. Every central function, every governance mechanism, every capital allocation decision must demonstrably add value that subsidiaries could not create alone.

Digital is not a pillar — it is the atmosphere. Every subsidiary strategy must be digitally native. We will invest SAR 400 million over five years in digital transformation across the group.

Nora Al-Rashid Group CEO, Cultural Assets Group



3. WHO WE ARE — MISSION, VISION & VALUES

3.1 Mission Statement

"To preserve, activate, and scale cultural assets for the enrichment of communities and the creation of sustainable economic value."

3.2 Vision Statement

"By 2028, CAG will be the Middle East and North Africa's leading cultural economy group — recognized for the authenticity of our cultural offerings, the excellence of our operations, and the impact of our investments on communities and stakeholders."

3.3 Core Values

Value

Definition

Behavioral Anchor

Authenticity

We honor the integrity of cultural assets and never compromise heritage for short-term gain

Every product/experience must pass the "Cultural Integrity Review"

Excellence

We pursue operational and creative excellence in everything we do

Zero tolerance for mediocrity; continuous improvement embedded in KPIs

Stewardship

We are custodians, not owners, of cultural assets — we hold them in trust for future generations

Long-term value creation over short-term extraction

Collaboration

We believe the group is greater than the sum of its parts

Cross-subsidiary projects are rewarded; silos are actively dismantled

Courage

We take bold, calculated bets on the future of culture

Innovation budget ring-fenced; failure-tolerant experimentation encouraged

3.4 Strategic Identity Summary

CAG is a strategic holding company (not a financial holding or passive investor). We actively shape subsidiary strategies, allocate capital with conviction, provide shared services where scale advantages exist, and intervene when subsidiaries underperform. Our parenting style is best described as "Strategic Architect" — we set the blueprint, resource the build, and monitor progress, but we empower subsidiary CEOs to lead execution.



4. OUR THEORY OF VALUE CREATION (PARENTING PURPOSE)

4.1 The Parenting Advantage Framework

CAG creates value for its subsidiaries through five mechanisms:

#

Value Creation Mechanism

Description

Example

1

Capital Allocation

Centralized capital allocation enables investment in highest-return opportunities across the portfolio, rather than each subsidiary self-funding

SAR 120M redirected from Subsidiary 4 (mature, cash-generative) to Subsidiary 2 (high-growth, capital-hungry) in 2023

2

Talent & Leadership Development

Group-wide talent pool, leadership rotation program, and centralized executive recruitment

Group CHRO manages top-50 leadership pipeline; 3 subsidiary CEOs rotated in 2022–2023

3

Shared Services & Scale Economies

Centralized procurement, finance, legal, IT infrastructure, and marketing analytics

Group procurement saved SAR 45M in FY2023 through consolidated vendor contracts

4

Brand & Reputation Halo

The CAG brand provides credibility, government access, and partnership leverage that individual subsidiaries could not achieve alone

CAG brand enabled Subsidiary 1 to secure a 25-year government concession valued at SAR 800M

5

Strategic Synergy Orchestration

Active identification and execution of cross-subsidiary revenue and cost synergies

"Cultural Passport" product (cross-selling across Subsidiaries 1, 2, and 5) generated SAR 28M incremental revenue in FY2023

4.2 Corporate-Level Strategy

CAG's corporate-level strategy is a Related-Linked Diversification strategy. Our subsidiaries are linked by:

A common focus on cultural assets as the core resource

Shared customer segments (cultural tourists, experience seekers, government/institutional buyers)

Complementary capabilities (content creation, venue management, digital distribution, education)

Geographic overlap (primarily MENA, with selective international expansion)

We explicitly reject unrelated diversification. Any future acquisition or incubation must pass the "Cultural Nexus Test": Does this entity's core business fundamentally depend on, or contribute to, the cultural economy?



5. STRATEGIC CONTEXT & ENVIRONMENTAL SCAN

5.1 Macro-Environmental Analysis (PESTEL)

Factor

Key Trends

Implication for CAG

Time Horizon

Political

Saudi Vision 2030 allocating SAR 50B+ to culture & entertainment; UAE cultural investment accelerating; Egypt cultural heritage monetization

Massive tailwind; government as customer, partner, and regulator simultaneously

2024–2030

Economic

MENA GDP growth 3.2% (IMF 2024); tourism recovery post-COVID at 112% of 2019 levels; inflation moderating to 2.8%

Favorable demand environment; cost pressures easing

2024–2026

Social

Youth demographic bulge (65% under 35 in KSA); rising demand for experiential consumption; cultural identity as social currency

Core demand driver; product design must be youth-centric and Instagram-worthy

Structural

Technological

Generative AI transforming content creation; immersive tech (AR/VR) enabling new cultural experiences; blockchain for digital art/collectibles

Opportunity and threat; must invest or be disrupted

2024–2028

Environmental

ESG expectations rising; cultural tourism carbon footprint under scrutiny; green building standards for cultural venues

Must integrate sustainability into operations; potential competitive differentiator

2024–2028

Legal

Evolving IP frameworks in MENA; entertainment licensing reforms in KSA; data privacy regulations (PDPL)

Compliance investment required; IP protection critical for content subsidiaries

2024–2026

5.2 Industry Analysis — Cultural Economy Value Chain

The cultural economy value chain consists of four layers:

Cultural Asset Origination — Heritage sites, artistic creation, IP development

Cultural Asset Activation — Experiences, events, exhibitions, education

Cultural Asset Distribution — Digital platforms, media, licensing, merchandising

Cultural Asset Monetization — Ticketing, sponsorship, real estate, government contracts

CAG's portfolio spans all four layers, which is a distinctive competitive advantage. Most competitors operate in one or two layers.

5.4 SWOT Summary (Pre-Assessment — CEO's Perspective)



Positive

Negative

Internal

Strengths: Unique portfolio spanning full cultural value chain; strong government relationships; SAR 2.1B revenue base; talented subsidiary CEOs

Weaknesses: Synergies underexploited; digital maturity uneven across subsidiaries; holding company overhead questioned by some board members; financial reporting not yet fully consolidated in real-time

External

Opportunities: Vision 2030 cultural investment wave; digital/AI transformation of cultural experiences; international expansion (Egypt, Morocco, Turkey); "Cultural Passport" product scaling

Threats: Government entities competing directly; talent war for creative/tech professionals; regulatory uncertainty in new markets; economic downturn reducing discretionary cultural spending

KEY ORGANIZATIONAL OBSERVATIONS

Span of Control: Group CEO has 12 direct reports (6 GEC + 6 Subsidiary CEOs) — at the upper limit of effective span. Consider adding a Group Deputy CEO or COO with subsidiary oversight responsibility.

Saudization: Group-wide Saudization rate is 72% (target: 80% by 2026). Highest in Sub 4 (Arts Education, 85%) and lowest in Sub 3 (Digital Content, 55% — tech talent scarcity).

Gender Diversity: 34% female across group; 43% at GEC level (3 of 7); 33% at Subsidiary CEO level (2 of 6). Board: 22% female (2 of 9).

Average Tenure: GEC average tenure is 3.0 years (relatively new team). Subsidiary CEO average tenure is 3.5 years. Longest-serving: Dr. Mona Al-Turki (Sub 4, 5 years). Shortest: Yara Al-Amri (Group CMO, 1 year).

Holding Company Overhead: 120 FTE at SAR 42M cost represents 2.0% of group revenue. Benchmark for strategic holding companies is 1.5–2.5% — CAG is within range but should monitor as revenue scales.

Reporting Matrix: Subsidiary functional heads (Finance, HR) have a solid line to their Subsidiary CEO and a dotted line to the corresponding Group function head. This creates a matrix that enables group standards while preserving subsidiary autonomy. However, interviews suggest the dotted line is inconsistently enforced — some subsidiary Finance Directors have minimal interaction with the Group CFO.
